utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. We'll go ahead and hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, might I raise just one very small matter of evidence before the Defence start? It's a very minor matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It won't take a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, interviews were conducted with the defendants and they were tendered into evidence and they constitute Exhibits P138 to P142. They are two interviews with Mr. Tadic and three interviews with Mr. Zaric. The interviews as they currently stand consist of a written English translation. The Prosecution has prepared and will, not today but in the very near future, in the next few days, I hope, be able to produce reformatted interviews which will contain the English question, translated underneath into B/C/S, the B/C/S answer, and then the English answer. So a B/C/S reader will be able to look at the document and see the questions in B/C/S and the answers in B/C/S and an English reader will be able to do the same. And if it ever comes to asking the defendants about the content of those interviews, it will simply mean that they will also be able to read it simultaneously. I hope to have those documents ready within the next few days and to produce them into evidence if I may and I would hope to substitute them for the exhibits P138 to 142. So I raise that now and hope that the Defence would be able to indicate an attitude to my application. I shouldn't think there would be any objection, because it just helps everyone. It gives them the B/C/S and the English on the same page and is essentially much the same document as already exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I would imagine that the Defence would first like to see the documents and look at them and compare with the ones that have already been accepted and see whether or not they are indeed the same as you --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. I'll attend to all of those matters, make sure that they have seen them and got them. As I said, my prediction is there won't be any objection, but I just wanted to raise that matter and let the Chamber know, given that it's Prosecution material and that I'll be seeking to introduce it at this stage in the case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Just before we start, I would like to bring to the attention of this Trial Chamber a few matters. In fact, yesterday evening our second expert, Professor Nikolic, fortunately came into The Hague after the great, I would say, and I wish to thank them great efforts of the witness unit with regard to the problems with visa due to the previous schedule, et cetera, et cetera. Professor Nikolic, as I said, has very, very tough and very precise commitments in next few days, so in fact he should be in Belgrade at latest tomorrow, tomorrow morning. And I hope that we shall organise and finish that. Another matter: Since he came yesterday evening, after connecting flights, which was only available at that time, he is a gentleman 74 years old. He was quite exhausted. So I wasn't able yesterday to give him certain instructions, preparations, simply to familiarise him with this area here. So I would kindly suggest and kindly request this Trial Chamber: After we finish Professor Kecmanovic during the morning, then we shall have the break until the afternoon session in order to, you know, speak with witness, prepare him, you know, with these topics, and then we shall proceed as scheduled at 2.30 afternoon. And then we could have enough time to finish all examination of Professor Nikolic today, and then he could be able to leave tomorrow. So I would say two flights in 48 hours he can resolve it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Another matter, Your Honour, if you allow me. It is regarding Professor Kecmanovic. Recently it came to the attention of the Defence that in one magazine or journal from Sarajevo, certain portions of his expert opinion was published. Defence acted in accordance with the standards of our code of conduct, professional code of conduct, and we sent a fax to the Sarajevo journal, Sarajevo newspaper. In that fax, we explicitly requested that the content of that fax and the explanations with regard to this particular case should not be published by any way until the final response and final result of all this inquiry. In spite of that very clear request from the side of Defence, in the same newspaper, our fax was published, in total. Since we are facing here with to some extent quite significant and important issue, I kindly ask this Trial Chamber to launch certain investigation with regard to the so-called leaking of information from certain parts of this institution, whether it's registry or - I don't know - the other parts. Anyhow, the Sarajevo newspaper should give explanations how and when they came into the possession of certain portions of Professor Kecmanovic's report. Not to mention that the first article was published only a couple of days before multiparty elections in Bosnia, where Professor Kecmanovic was one of the candidates in Croatian Muslim Federation, Federation of B and H. But I will leave it to the other party. It's not important for the moment. I gave to Translation Unit one copy of this fax that we sent, and just for the record, it's fairly short. I would like to read it out and to inform Trial Chamber about the response of the newspaper and then officially we shall start with the filing -- if Trial Chamber will instruct us to make further steps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour? So the article which was published recently, it was on 25th of October this year, in Bosnian magazine called Dani, "Days." Meaning in English "Days." On the page 16, they -- maybe I can have the assistance of Ms. Usher, please. If you can put on the ELMO -- although I will read. Thank you. Well, the title of this article is "Sarajevo with love, second part." I will read in Serbian language. This is the content of our fax. [Interpretation] "We have recently learned that in your esteemed newspaper, on the 3rd of October, 2002, on page 12, a story was published under the headline 'Nenad Kecmanovic, to Sarajevo with love.' In the mentioned text, the following circumstance is mentioned: That Professor Kecmanovic, author of the report that is being used in case IT-95-9-T before the Tribunal in The Hague. Bearing in mind that the Defence team in the mentioned case will soon start presenting its evidence, including the testimony of Professor Kecmanovic, we kindly request you to send us a fax within eight days after they receive this fax, namely, the following information: Number 1, who was the author of the text that was published on 3rd of October, 2002 on page 12 of your newspaper? Number 2, who, when, and in which way learned about the participation of Professor Kecmanovic before the Tribunal in The Hague as a Defence expert in the mentioned case? And number 3: In which way and from whom did your paper come into the possession of the contents of the document that is authored by Professor Kecmanovic? "In this way, we inform you that the procedure before The Hague Tribunal, in accordance with the rules of procedure that are enforced, under certain conditions and in certain cases, including this one, is close to the public and protected by the principle of confidentiality. In view of this fact, there are indications that court procedure has been jeopardised by your discovery of the above-mentioned information. This circumstance is of essential importance for the further proceedings, so we request you most kindly to give us your answer within the above-mentioned deadline. "Finally, we wish to inform you that this letter is confidential in accordance with the standards of the Tribunal in The Hague and that it is not allowed to transmit its contents to third persons who are not directly involved in the events concerned, and also it is not allowed to publish it in any form in the public media. Respectfully yours, on behalf of the Defence team, Igor Pantelic." "Dear Mr. Pantelic --" now, the answer is the following: "Dear Mr. Pantelic, I wish to inform you that our magazine is not going to grant your request. We are sincerely surprised by your request, in view of the fact that we assume that you are familiar with the procedure of the Tribunal. If you really believe that there are indications that by publishing this text, in respect of which you are addressing us, we have violated the procedure of the Tribunal, we would like to ask you to address the organ of the Tribunal that is in charge of assessing, under quotation marks, 'indications,' on violations of procedure. At the same time, I wish to avail myself of this opportunity to inform you on this occasion that without mediation of the competent organ of the Tribunal, our magazine is not interested in cooperating with you. Respectfully yours, Vildana Selimbegovic." [In English] So Your Honour, in this particular case, we think that somehow the portions of the witness expert report came to the attention of the third side. We don't have any particular problem with the particular testimony of this witness here today in the Tribunal. This is a public hearing, of course. But we are very concerned about the possibility that media might be in possession of certain documents or portions of documents or - I don't know - evidences in this particular case that we are dealing. So I kindly and respectfully ask this Trial Chamber to instruct the relevant institutions or departments of this Tribunal and to launch certain investigation with regard, and Defence will be of assistance in any sense. Thank you for your attention, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Pantelic. The Trial Chamber will consider the matter and give instructions in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we proceed? Can the witness be -- take the solemn declaration, please. Can he stand up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Professor Kecmanovic.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you please come closer to the microphone so that the interpreters could hear you. Thank you. Professor, we have your curriculum vitae. We are not going to go into the details of your rich career. We have been instructed by the Trial Chamber as to how to conduct this examination today after this series of questions, our learned friends from the Prosecution are going to question you, and of course the Trial Chamber is there if they may have any questions for you. First and foremost, could you tell us when you were born and where?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 9th of September, 1947, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You have a degree in political science from the University of Sarajevo and you graduated in 1975; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My mistake. That is actually when you got your doctorate in 1975; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And you got your bachelor's degree in 1971; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And you got your master's degree in 1973?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I had two majors at the faculty of political science. One is sociology and the other one is political science.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You come from a family of intellectuals. What was your father?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: He wrote about the theory of literature and culture. He was a critic and he was a member of the academy of sciences and arts of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What about your mother?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: She was a professor of classical languages. She taught Greek and Latin at the Sarajevo high school.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your grandfather, what was your grandfather?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: He was a priest and a politician. He was a senator in the Yugoslavia between the two world wars, in the kingdom of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... concerns the Trial Chamber now is that of the witness, and we have it in writing. It's been filed. Can we move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will take care about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, tell me: Your immediate family has lived in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina for how long?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: The Kecmanovic's have been living in Bosnia-Herzegovina for generations. They originate from Bosnia Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: For how long?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Four or five generations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You were a member of the collective presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In which period was this?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: This was in June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me: After that you were no longer there?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you resign?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I resigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You were president of the party of reformists in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was the party that was called the union of reform forces for Bosnia-Herzegovina, and at the level of all of Yugoslavia, it was led by then prime minister Ante Markovic and I was president of the party in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Recently you were a candidate at the elections in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On behalf of which party?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: On behalf of the independent social democrats of Milorad Dodik. I was candidate of that party in the elections in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: During the communist regime, you were suspected by the regime of cooperating with foreign intelligence services. Could you tell us a few words about that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This had to do with the elections for the last presidency, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I was one of the candidates for the presidency from Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was the candidate with the largest number of votes. However, just before the election procedure was about to be brought to an end, the public -- the state security service insinuated that I had suspicious links with the West, and this grew into charges for espionage. And then I was eliminated from the elections procedure. Immediately after that, this was called a lack of security culture, so it did not affect my status, apart from this candidacy. I remained director of the university, member of the League of Communists, and quite simply, there were no consequences to be borne, except for the fact that I was eliminated from the elections procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You also taught at various universities abroad; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at several universities. I lectured at several universities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you please mention some of them.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Innsbruck, Budapest, Khartoum, Grand Valley State University in Michigan, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, maybe I can explain. The transcript was not 100 per cent accurate. We heard from the witness that he remained also the director of the university, and we haven't found this in the transcript. So just a matter of accuracy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. Maybe you can deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will clarify. Yes, Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, this was not part of the transcript. After this episode with some insinuations, if I can put it that way, vis-a-vis your personality, you remained director of the university in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I pointed that out so that it would be clear this was an insinuation. I said that when this espionage affair came to its peak, as it was then called in the media, I was directly accused of espionage. However, at the moment when every possibility was eliminated for me to be a candidate further, then everything was returned to the previous state of affairs, and then this qualification was just brought down to some general assessment that I had a shortage or lack of security culture, which meant nothing in a formal sense. And the proof that all of this was simply construed was that there was no action that followed. And this would have had to be proven. And inter alia, I remained rector of the university and I kept all the other public positions I had, including my membership in the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, that is to say, in the ruling party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Also here before the Tribunal, you gave evidence in two cases. You gave your expert opinion. As far as I can see, this is Kvocka, Prijedor, and also the Krnojelac Foca case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's -- the question is: You gave evidence. Could he please explain what you mean by gave evidence? I don't believe this man has ever testified. He might have filed reports, and he was never used as a witness. That might be closer to the truth. Could they please clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's a question of being specific as to what services --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. When you say gave evidence, filing a report can be giving evidence or giving testimony. I don't believe this man has ever testified. I don't think his reports were ever used. He might have filed them, but ....

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. In order to spare time it's a question of translation. I asked him whether he filed a report, not gave evidence. So it's a matter of translation. I will clarify that. No problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, Professor, let's clarify this for the transcript. You in fact did not appear, did not testify live here before the Trial Chamber in any other case; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So you simply wrote a report and then Defence teams in those cases sent it and took care of it later on. So you were not invited here to come and testify. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please tell me: You have heard and you are probably aware that immediately before this year's elections, this article was published in the newspaper Dani. What is your position? What is your personal viewpoint regarding the fact that this appeared immediately before your coming to testify here and that it had this type of heading?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object. What is the relevance to this? I've never read the article. I don't believe any member of our Prosecution team has read the article and it's a public document, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The relevance, Your Honour, is from the point of view of the Defence is that Professor Kecmanovic, being a witness, expert witness for the Defence, might be, might be to some extent concerned or, well, I don't know, not to say intimidated, but let's hear him here, because maybe that would be a part of the evidence for the further procedures. After all, he's a witness. He's entitled just to give here his opinion what was his feelings about all these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, Mr. Pantelic. This witness has come in to support his expert opinion which has been filed, and that's what we are dealing with now. The Trial Chamber has not decided that it's going to conduct an inquiry into this matter which you raised with the magazine. So we are not going to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. And another matter -- I've finished with these several questions according to the instructions of the Trial Chamber. Your Honour, the Defence is in quite a serious situation, because initially when we filed our briefs regarding the potential exhibits which might be tendered into these proceedings, well, we were not of the opinion that our expert witnesses will give the evidence with regard to the Defence only in this limited way. So there is a number of, well, from the point of view of Defence, significant exhibits that we have on our lists, and now we are prevented to introduce them as the exhibits. So with your permission, maybe we could do that at later stage, or now, but in any case, when the witness is here, just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Are there -- what I want to know is: Are there exhibits attached to the expert opinion report of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, not on that way. We have certain documents, certain exhibits where this particular witness can give his personal opinion and professional opinion, and then we could tender it into evidence, with regard to the relevant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We cannot mix procedures like that, because if an expert witness has got exhibits which he or she wants to discuss in the report, they are always attached to the report and discussed in the opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But on the other hand we have certain, I would say, common or universal exhibits. For example, these are the extracts from the Official Gazette or from several sources. So we need certain verification, expert verification, of this kind of exhibits. So in that sense, I thought that maybe it would be appropriate for the Defence to submit certain portions of this exhibit and then see the opinion of the expert witness and then this document can be tendered. It's a kind of -- you know, it's very difficult to put only the report. These are only parts of the certain legislation which is of importance for these proceedings. For example, we filed certain memorandum of the assembly of socialist Republic Bosnia and Herzegovina from 1991. We made a translation. We gave it to the Prosecution. It is a crucial and important document for this proceedings with regard to the events, chain of events in Bosnia. And furthermore, we were of the opinion and of the impression, following the practice with, for example, expert opinion, expert report on the Prosecution side, that during the examination of our expert witness, we could ask for certain clarification or a detailed or additional opinion about certain very, very important moments in this life, political life in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And now we are prevented. So what I'm asking, only to pass through these several documents, hear the opinion of our expert witness, and then it is to this Trial Chamber to decide whether this evidence will be accepted. Because, as I said, part of these exhibits are on our list previously filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to add a sentence to what my colleague Pantelic said. If you remember during the cross-examination of Mr. Donia, the Defence was allowed to tender in some documents that were not part of the expert opinion per se, but did pertain to certain parts of that expert opinion. This is why I think that this is a further argument that corroborates what Mr. Pantelic said. We didn't expect that we would not be able to lead the chief examination of the witness, and this applies not only to Professor Kecmanovic but to other expert witnesses. And if such witnesses do have knowledge, information of these matters, then this is the only way to tender in such documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, it seems to the Trial Chamber that during the Prosecution case, all the documents that their experts discussed were attached to the report and were actually discussed in the report and the Defence, because they were cross-examining, that's why they were allowed to bring in other documents to ask the expert witness. But in this case, your witness prepared this report and didn't attach any exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, well, as far as the Defence is concerned, we have, I would say, certain well-known facts, for example, legislation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And I'm wondering --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Which we'll discuss Your Honour in many occasions with other witnesses too. So it is not strictly related to this particular witness, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. When you filed in your list of exhibits, did you indicate which witnesses are going to discuss those exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, not yet. We have to reorganise maybe certain number of exhibits. We shall cut in order to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. But for this particular expert witness, there are no exhibits attached in his report, so you can't discuss any other exhibits which are not in the report. Because this is an expert opinion. It is not a fact witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, his expert opinion -- he's an expert witness, of course, but maybe his personal knowledge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Limited -- as far as the Trial is concerned, it is limited to the report which has been filed before the Trial Chamber. Because there's no other notice that he's an expert in other fields as well. It's only limited to the report which has been filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, you know what the problem is with this approach: The Defence was quite surprised when we realised that we shall not be able to lead this witness in chief. In that case, Your Honour, we would be -- I'm not speaking about -- Your Honour, please allow me just to finish my words. We were not, Your Honour -- it is not -- it was not our intention to tender into evidence certain documents there, because we would seek from this witness one additional explanations about certain points which are important for our case. That's one matter. And therefore, we were not in a situation to attach certain number of the documents, since we have explanations in the report. Now, Your Honour, this is a new situation. Therefore, I kindly ask you and respectfully ask you to allow us to pass certain portions of the legislation and certain documents, because the Defence now is, according to the instruction and the ruling of this Honourable Trial Chamber, prevented to lead this witness in chief. So that's the bottom line, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's not correct, Mr. Pantelic. That's not correct. If what you wanted was to discuss the highlights of the opinion, that you can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But the point is, this witness is limited only to discuss matters which are in his expert report which has been filed. That is the limitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And that is why I'm saying that he can't discuss exhibits which have not been attached to his report where there is no indication that this expert witness is going to discuss those exhibits. If what you want is to highlight certain aspects of the opinion of this witness, that you can do, but not to bring in things which are not in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In fact, that is my idea, and I am satisfied with this approach, Your Honour. And then we could see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe you misunderstood what an expert witness's role is all about in any given case. You can go ahead, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Limited to the opinion report which has been filed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will do that, Your Honour, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor Kecmanovic, let us just cover a few of these points. Tell me, please: You were chairman of the party of reformists in 1991, in October of 1991?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And your party was represented in the assembly of the then socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, after the first free elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How many deputies did your party have in the assembly of BH?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And who was the head of your group of deputies?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, it was first Dragan Kalinic, and later on it was Sefudin Tokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What seems to be important, both in your report and for the Defence case, is the time in the middle of October when deputies of Serb ethnicity left the assembly. I would like to ask you now: What parties did those Serb deputies represent, the ones that left the BH assembly in October of 1991?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: The premise -- they left the premises of the assembly that evening before the elections. Members of the SDS and also a large number of Serbs who were members of other parties, multinational parties, meaning the party of reformists, that I was a member of, and SDP, which is the reformist party of communists, and also other smaller parties. Not all of the Serbs left those parties, but a large majority did. I would also like to say that in addition to the Serbs who were members of the SDS, there were other 13 Serbs who were deputies in the assembly and who represented other multinational parties. There were also Muslims and Croats who were deputies but did not represent the three national parties: SDS, SDA, and HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to slow down a little bit for the sake of interpreters. You and I speak the same language, so we need to bear this in mind. What was the main reason for what happened on the 14th and 15th October of 1991, when the deputies of Serb nationality left the multiparty and multi-ethnic assembly of BH?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: As I explained in my expert opinion, there was a key moment in the political fate of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that was that event, which in a way violated the constitutional order. We can even say that the basic principle, constitutional principle of equality and constitutionality of people was violated, which prompted them to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he has a background in political science and sociology. I have no objection to him discussing his political views, political opinions, or giving us some insight into the history of what occurred. However, with regard to describing constitutional violations, there is no evidence that he is a constitutional scholar, has any legal background or training. He is not an expert in that area. That's outside the scope of his expertise, and we would move to strike any comments that he has in relation to constitutional violations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. That objection is sustained, because, like I said, I did say he should discuss only what is within his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: He was there, Your Honour, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but he's not a fact witness. Can we stick to what the expert report contains, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And if you think that you are through with any highlights in the opinion report, then that's the end of your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have only one matter and I will finish, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So please tell me, in view of the fact that you're an expert in political sciences and humanities: So based on your professional expertise and education, and since you are also a connoisseur of political situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, please tell us this: When the memorandum and platform of BH were adopted without the presence of Serb deputies in the assembly, what were the consequences of that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: If I can just add to what we discussed previously. This event that you brought up and which I tried to assess, we don't have to look at it only from the constitutional point of view. We can also look at it from the political point of view. This was one of the fateful events in the history of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it was a political fact. Let's leave the constitutional aspect of it aside. The constitutionality of people, the status of the constitutional status of people, was violated. At that time, Bosnia and Herzegovina was defined as a republic which was neither Croat nor Serb nor Muslim, but all of these three together. This was a political principle that was very important for the political functioning of all three peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And up until that moment, this principle was upheld, even in that assembly, regardless of numerous conflicts that existed between political parties. Up until that time, this principle was upheld, and it held the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina together, in a way. The consequence -- the political consequences of that are well known. In my opinion, this caused a break-up, and the Serb party, upon facing the fact that it was ignored by other two sides, left the joint administration and organs of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what happened with Croats?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as the Croatian side is concerned, the later events showed that this was some kind of a tactical support, because soon after the SDS left the assembly, the HDZ started establishing its own autonomous administration in western Herzegovina, in Posavina, and other parts of the republic that held Croatian -- that had Croatian majority. Later on there was also a conflict between the HVO and the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was predominantly a Muslim party, and all of this led to the break-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The political act of separation, however, had been carried out much earlier. So at that time, the break-up actually started, and later on three national administrations were established in Bosnia and Herzegovina which covered their own territory, and this is why, in my expert report, I stated that from that moment on, three states started -- or three state administrations started functioning in Bosnia and Herzegovina. All of them had their own assemblies, their executive organs, their armies, their territory. And naturally, they waged a war against each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I would ask you to slow down so that the interpreters can catch up.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will attempt to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Professor, another item that we need to cover is the effort of the international community to bring about a peaceful resolution of the conflict. This pertains to Cutilheiro's plan in February of 1992. What is your professional and expert position regarding this second crucial moment in the so-called Bosnian drama?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. We could call this the second crucial and dramatic moment in its fate. Since I have -- since I appear here as an expert witness, not as a fact witness, I will try to disregard the fact that I was a participant in these events. And at the time, it was believed that there was a resolution in sight. The negotiations went on for quite a while. Some of them took place in Sarajevo, some in Lisbon, in the Sarajevo phase of negotiations, opposition parties were included as well, although marginally, as was the party that I represented in those negotiations. It seemed that the resolution of the crisis was near, especially when the news arrived from Lisbon that there was -- that a principled agreement on the internal order of Bosnia-Herzegovina had been reached and that the main issue had been solved, namely, that Radovan Karadzic and the SDS, and those Serbs who were in Lisbon negotiating there, that they accepted -- or they agreed that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be recognised as an independent state. And that was quite important, because that was the first time that the Serb side had agreed that Bosnia-Herzegovina should exist as an independent state. This is especially important because up until then the Serb side had insisted on the continuity of Bosnia and Herzegovina and wished Bosnia-Herzegovina to remain within Yugoslavia. So in a way, this represented a change in the position of the Serb party, a compromise on their behalf, and they agreed to this despite the results of the plebiscite. On the other hand, the Muslim side accepted, or shall we say gave up, this reciprocal compromise, gave up on it, and gave up on the unitarian internal structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina that they had supported up until then. So it seemed that these multilateral concessions made the compromise possible and that the worst consequence that everyone feared, which was the internal interethnic conflict, was avoided. And soon thereafter, we received the news that the Muslim leader and president of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time, who also at the time represented the Muslim side in negotiations, withdrew his signature. What is most interesting and most important about this - and I will conclude this - is that this arrangement that had been approved, initialed in Lisbon, was not different from what later was signed in Dayton. The huge difference, of course, that is what happened -- is that it happened three and a half years later, after many victims and much destruction. Some experts, such as Warren Zimmerman, and I can use his opinion, which probably would be supported by the analysis, is that Muslim or later on Bosniak side, that for them the Lisbon arrangement was in fact more favourable than the Dayton arrangement that ensued later on. That's my commentary to what you brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Dayton. What is the parallel between the Cutilheiro plan and the Dayton Agreement? What is this parallel that you wish to highlight? Just briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, the parallel lies in the following: First of all, in the method of seeking agreement from the Lisbon negotiations all the way up to the Dayton negotiations, in the talks, as protagonists, it is not the representatives of the institutions of Bosnia-Herzegovina that appear. It is not members of the presidency belonging to the three ethnic groups. It is not ministers or MPs. These are actually delegations of the three ruling parties, the three national delegations. It is interesting that this move in these first negotiations under the auspices of the European Union already then, in a way, sidetracked the institutions of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The delegations were headed by Izetbegovic, who was the only one who was a member of the presidency, and he was the top man in the presidency, but also Karadzic and Boban, who held no state functions whatsoever. All ensuing negotiations were conducted on the basis of that principle, this being concluded by Dayton. As for the substance involved, in Lisbon and later in Dayton, an internal decentralisation was carried out, an internal division. As cantons were referred to previously, in Dayton we have an addition to this. Perhaps I could put it that way. In addition to the cantons, we have entities as well. Of course, what is particularly noteworthy is the fact that this is a new structure of central joint organs that function on the basis of the principle of parity, consensus, the national right to veto, a Chamber of nations in the parliament. So there are many analogies, but the differences are related to certain percentages in the territorial division.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that in Bosnia, before the war, before 1992, in this political system, and then in relation to the Cutilheiro plan and in relation to Dayton, the principle of the vital interest of peoples was protected in the same way? Is that your claim?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, in the period -- the communist period, or rather, in the socialist period, this principle, this tenet that I referred to earlier on, I didn't want to go into constitutional subject-matter, so let us call it a basic principle. It functioned or rather it was implemented in a different way, since there was a one-party system in place. What was strictly observed was the so-called national key in the distribution of political offices among the members of the three national ethnic groups. However, crucial matters were resolved within one party, which greatly insisted upon this element of the fact that all three peoples were constituent and what was constantly invoked was the formula that I already mentioned, namely, that Bosnia-Herzegovina is neither Serb nor Croat nor Muslim, but that rather it belongs to all three. I think that a great problem cropped up in the first post-communist government, because in a different situation of multiparty elections, democratic elections, et cetera, firmer mechanisms of equality of rights were not ensured. The principle of veto, or rather, the principle of consensus, was not introduced in the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, at the moment when I joined the presidency, I put forth as a prerequisite the right of veto, that is to say, decision-making by consensus. Quite simply, this was the only way to make it impossible to have one national group outvoted by the other or others. Two sides against one. A reserve mechanism, so to speak, existed only in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There was no Chamber of nationalities, but it was to be introduced in Dayton. However, what existed was a council for national equality. It was a kind of substitute for a chamber of national groups or peoples. Annex 70, I believe, introduced this in the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, the socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was dwindling away, namely, that if the principle of equality is infringed upon, 20 MPs in parliament can ask, by tendering their signatures, can ask the speaker of parliament, the president of parliament, to remove a particular topic from the agenda, without any further debate. Then the entire problem would be referred to this council for national equality, which was constituted on the basis of the principle of parity again, an equal number for all national or ethnic groups, and every national or ethnic delegation had a right to veto. This mechanism -- that is one more thing I wish to add -- or actually, matters are sent back to parliament from this consensus only -- from this council only if something is agreed upon by consensus, or to put it even more specifically, the final wording that will be voted on in parliament subsequently is provided by that council. This mechanism, on several occasions in this parliament, was activated successfully, or rather, efficiently, from the moment the assembly was constituted all the way up to its break-up, that is to say, until the war broke out. However, that night, I believe it was crucial for political life in Bosnia-Herzegovina and its recent history, this principle was infringed upon. Quite simply, the intervention of 20 MPs, that the problem be transferred to the council for interethnic equality, or rather, national equality, was simply not accepted. That was a precedent in that sense. And this infringed upon the principle of equality. There is another interesting point in relation to that body. In a way, it was a phantom body. The council for national equality was actually never constituted. However, it was not necessary for that to be done in order for it to yield certain effects. Namely, as soon as 20 members of parliament would file an objection stating that national or ethnic equality was being infringed upon, the particular item was removed from the agenda. And since it went without saying, or was assumed, rather, that one of the three national delegations had been infringed upon, this would definitely be taken off the agenda. So it was not even necessary for that body to be constituted. It did function very well nevertheless. I believe that this is yet further proof of how important this principle of national equality was for the survival and proper functioning of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Finally, Professor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. Because I think we've got all the details. You should wind up now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. Just one question with regard to that issue and I'm finished. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned the presidency, the collective presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Please be so kind as to tell the Trial Chamber and us, briefly, about this collective presidency in the period from April 1992 until July 1992, that is to say, the period while you were on the presidency, and also, possibly, if you have any knowledge as to who this presidency represented. Then I have another question: Which territory did this presidency and its institutions control, and how did this presidency function within the institution itself? This is an outline of what I would like you to tell us about. So if you could bring it all together within one answer, and this would conclude the examine in chief and then the prosecutor will continue.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: In my previous remarks, I already emphasised the problem that had to do with the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Namely, according to the Prosecution -- I beg your pardon for referring to matters that I am not competent for once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think the counsel simply asked you to describe how the presidency functioned. During the period that counsel referred to.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: That is precisely what I had embarked upon. I do thank you. It functioned by majority vote. That was the principle involved. This was the process in which there was constant outvoting at a 2:1 ratio. This was a stage in which the representatives of the Muslim side, to be more had precise, the candidates of the Party of Democratic Action and the Croat representatives, or rather, to be more precise, the candidates, the members of the presidency who were elected from the HDZ list, they acted together, in opposition to the Serb side and the representatives of the SDS. Of course, later on, as events evolved, alliances changed and there were new confrontations. However, in that period, that was the balance of forces involved, if I could put it that way. Since the majority principle of decision-making was in force, the Serb side was constantly being outvoted. At the moment when I entered the presidency, or when, according to the constitutional law, I was supposed to enter the presidency as the third-ranking person from the list from the elections, because beforehand Mrs. Plavsic and the late Mr. Koljevic withdrew from the presidency, bearing in mind this experience, I insisted upon the following: That as a prerequisite for my acceptance of this office, the principle of consensus be introduced in its work. In addition to this request, this was not only a request of mine; it was also a request put forth by the fourth-ranking person, Mr. Pejanovic. We asked for consensus as a prerequisite for our work in the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and after certain contemplation we did receive a favourable answer. However, in practice, that's not the way it happened. This principle was practically sidestepped. Quite simply, when Mr. Pejanovic and I, either one or the other, or most often both of us together, would express in our discussions certain reservations vis-a-vis a particular proposal, then the chairman, knowing or feeling that this would be followed by a veto, would remove the item from the agenda, stating that it was insufficiently prepared and that therefore a consensus could not be reached. Then, afterwards, he would put it on the agenda of sessions that the two of us did not attend, or these sessions were scheduled at such a time that everybody knew we could not be present. Or, quite simply, because of the war situation, we could not receive invitations to attend the session in good time. However, even more drastic things happened, in terms of this anomaly in our work, as compared to the principles agreed upon. For example, in this period when I was on the presidency, one morning in the newspapers I read that an alliance was made between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, specifically Tudjman and Izetbegovic had signed an agreement on a military alliance. Beforehand, I had not heard about this at all at the presidency, and I raised that question that very same morning. The answer of the presiding member was that first of all this is just a canard that was launched by the newspapers. When I insisted that this should be seriously dealt with, because it was a serious matter that had to be seriously denied, the explanation I was given was that that is not exactly the way it was, or rather --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, we seem to go going into the nitty-gritty details, and that is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, let us just conclude, please. I asked you about the presidency controlling a particular military force. It was commander at that point in time. I'm asking you which part of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina did this army control at the beginning of the war in 1992? Can you give us a percentage on the basis of your own knowledge? And this would conclude this part of the examination. Just be brief, please.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was about 30 per cent of the territory, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't have further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And you are submitting the report and the c.v. as exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That is correct. I have a copy here for the -- do you need --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We all have copies. We just have to get the numbers. Can we have the numbers, please, for the c.v. and then the report.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The expert report will be treated as D53/1, and the c.v. will be D53A/1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: My name is Phillip Weiner. I represent the Office of the Prosecutor and I'm going to ask you some questions. Now, the report that you just filed, did you prepare that report yourself?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had co-workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you or the co-workers do the research on that report?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The research to provide information for that report, was that done by you or the co-workers?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Which type of research? That's what I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The newspapers that you cited, the books that you cited and quoted, that type of research.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: This was done by my co-workers, under my instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, did you check the citations or did your co-workers check the citations, investigate them, to determine if they were correct so you would have a valid report?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And as part of that, did you corroborate any of the information that you described, any of the incidents, to determine that that information was in fact valid or correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to tell me what you are specifically referring to. Could you give me the paragraph involved? It will be easier that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I was asking you on a general basis, but we will get into paragraphs, sir. Did you corroborate the information in that report, the facts in that report, to determine that it was correct before you placed it in that report?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, if I manage to understand you correctly, as regards a series of events that occurred in the period that we dealt with in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there are different opinions, different reports, different assessments, et cetera, because, of course, I made a selection among those results. I could not mention all sources and all contradictory information involved, but I simply pointed to some particular information, and therefore, I would be glad if we could discuss this in concrete terms, because then I could give you concrete answers as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine. Now, let us move on. Let's go to paragraphs 95 and 96 of your report. Do you have that in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll help you out with it. What I'm referring to is the February 5th, 1994 explosion at the Markale marketplace in central Sarajevo. Do you see what I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in your report, you quote a 1994 London Times report that a UN investigation had established, beyond doubt, that the mortar shell was fired from inside the Muslim lines. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is one of the assessments, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you further state, sir -- or I'll summarise it. The Muslims would fire on their own people and blame the Serbs. And you noted that the Serbs denied their involvement in that February 5th incident. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, as part of your research, as a professor and an author, did you ever read or analyse or review that United Nations report that was referred to in the London Times? Did you go to the direct source and review that report, sir?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, as far as paragraph 95 is concerned -- or rather, this is the way in which we made our presentation, not only on the basis of -- not only with regard to this subject. You will see that we quoted various opinions. I, as an author, am not making any assertions. I am mentioning different facts and I'm just insisting on the fact that there were different opinions with regard to particular matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: On that matter, you indicated that a London Times report stated that a UN investigation had established, beyond doubt, that the mortar shell was fired from inside the Muslim lines. Did you review that report, sir? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. But I have to point out, if you allow me, that it's not only the Times of London that provided this information. Right this minute I cannot give the other sources of information, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. Isn't it a fact that the United Nations report never held the Muslim army responsible for that explosion? Isn't that true, sir, that your report is wrong?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I do not go beyond what is said here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you want to take the break now or should I confront him with the report, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Just one question. In fact, to you, Mr. Weiner. If the witness, as he has stated, did not go to the primary source and did not actually read the UN report, then he obviously can't know what's in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's what I want to confront him. I have the copies in B/C/S here. I want to show it to him and show that it's all a fiction, his statement or his opinion is based on fiction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It's based on the London Times, the Times of London.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Which was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So your report, therefore, is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would you like to take the break now, Your Honour, or should we continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We'll take the break now and continue at 11.30 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examination continuing. I did say you continue, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Madam Usher I have copies in both English and B/C/S of the UN report -- investigative report. If you could put the English one on the video and give the witness a B/C/S copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't see any relevance for that, because Professor Kecmanovic replied that the sources was the newspaper, and he said that he never consulted or looked into these documents, so I don't see any particular reason why we should go or establish what is in this report, because from the answers of our expert witness, it's very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The objection is overruled. The Prosecution will proceed. It is relevant because the newspaper cited this particular UN report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Professor, and members of the Court, I invite your attention to paragraph 17, please, on the third page. Sir, I have in front of you the United Nations report on the Sarajevo market explosion of 5 February 1994. This is an initial report which the newspaper commented on. Now, if we look at paragraph 17, there is no indication in that paragraph, as you indicated in your report from the London Times that the mortar shell was fired from inside the Muslim lines. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, let us continue. Are you aware that General Galic, of the Bosnian Serb army, has been indicted for that incident of 5 February 1994? Are you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that General Galic is currently being tried here at this Tribunal, not in this courtroom but here at this Tribunal for that crime which was committed on the 5th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that. However, based on the paragraph that was just quoted by you from the UN report, there is no specific finding as to culpability. It remains open that either side could have been culpable in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, let us move on to that. Are you aware that in the Galic trial, testimony has been introduced linking the explosion to the Bosnian Serb army, linking the shell coming from the Bosnian Serb army, and basically linking that to General Galic? Are you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. But I know that there is a trial going on against General Galic. However, it hasn't been completed yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I realise it hasn't been completed, sir, but are you aware that the Trial Chamber in the Galic case has recently ruled that the Prosecution has presented sufficient evidence that a reasonable trier of fact could convict General Galic on that incident? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. We are getting into the legal issues 98 bis rulings and all other standards, I don't believe that this witness can give any answer to these inquiries. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner. I think we are getting into territory where it's still unspecified, it's still not a concluded finding of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, sir -- then let me ask him this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Based on the information I presented to you, which shows that the article you cited to was incorrect, would you like to amend your report at this time and remove that paragraph or those two paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: The text that has been presented by you, for which I thank you, because it is the report of the UN, and item 17 does not specify who is culpable, which side was culpable. I encountered in the past assumptions indicating that this side was the culprit, or the other one, and that the culpability had not been established. I would not like to comment on the trial against General Galic, but that trial has not been completed yet. Therefore, it remains open what kind of a decision will be passed, and I would not like to get into that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, sir. I'm not asking -- that wasn't my question, sir. My question is: You based your report on information that was eight years old and that was incorrect. Having based your report on eight-year-old information that was incorrect, would you at this time like to amend or change your report? Because we know it's incorrect.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I would be willing to amend it once the trial of General Galic is completed and once all the facts are established. Until then, there are various assumptions that can stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, regardless of the assumptions, sir, nowhere in the United Nations report does it state it has been established beyond doubt that the mortar shell was fired from inside Muslim lines; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us continue. Could we move to paragraph 70, please. Sir, I would like to direct your attention to the third, fourth, and fifth sentences in paragraph 70. I'm sorry, the fourth, fifth, and sixth sentences: "Indeed --" I'll read them to you: "Indeed, the media pressure in the West was focused exclusively on the Serb side and its alleged atrocities against the Muslims. Early in August, in order to prove that the Serbs were not mistreating Muslims, Karadzic allowed the western media to freely inspect some detention camps. The result of this, however, was that Serbs were made to look even worse, as western television stations and the press competed on the basis of flimsy evidence, to present the Serbs as modern-day Nazis running extermination camps." Sir, what I'd like to talk to you about is the alleged atrocities and the flimsy evidence. Do you know which camps were visited by the journalists in that case or in that situation? Which camps were visited by the journalists when Karadzic allowed them to visit?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the camp in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That was one of them, sir. Can you think of any of the others?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Keraterm was another. Let me see if I can refresh your recollection as to the others. You've cited on at least seven occasions, either cited or quoted "Yugoslavia death of a nation," by Laura Silber and Allan Little; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me please read to you one paragraph which begins on the bottom of page 250 and continues through the top of page 251: "There were, it turned out, four large detention camps that gained international notoriety. Trnopolje and Manjaca were transit camps, where inmates lived in appalling conditions and were subject to random beatings and a sadistic whim of their guards. But in Omarska and Keraterm, a former ceramics factory on the outskirts of Prijedor, there was evidence that the prisoners were separated into categories based on interrogation. They were intimidated into giving evidenced against each other. After this screening process, they were placed in one of three categories: A, B, or C. In category A, those who were judged to have been leaders of the Muslim community or volunteers of one of the Bosnian militias or Territorial Defence. Most of these were killed. Category B consisted of men who were drafted into the Territorial Defence. And category C was all the rest. They were transferred to Trnopolje or elsewhere, where they would be held until they could be exchanged for Serbs, taken prisoner by the government forces, or for Serbs living on government-held territory who wanted to cross to the Serb side." In your opinion, sir, when you've published your opinion or your report, you didn't mention that information from a book by Silber and Little when you discussed the alleged atrocities and the flimsy evidence in paragraph 70.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: What's your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: My question is: Although you have quoted and cited the Laura and Silber book -- the Laura Silber and Allan Little book on several occasions, you did not mention that paragraph when you talked about not atrocities, not potential atrocities, but in your words, alleged atrocities.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: The book of Laura Silber and Allan Little has a chapter that I think is entitled, "The meeting between Izetbegovic and Krajisnik." Do you remember that chapter?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, that's not my question. My question to you is: Did you mention that information?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's quite important, this chapter. Let me remind you. It speaks about the fact that that was the last meeting between two leaders of two national sides, that it was tete-a-tete meeting and it also goes on to present the content of their conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's not my question. My question to you is: Did you mention the description of atrocities in that book in your report? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm saying now is supposed to indicate how authentic that text and that book is. I have direct knowledge that some parts of that book are not accurate, and I can confirm that. That meeting was not tete-a-tete. I was present there as well, and the content of the conversation was quite different. I was in fact the one who arranged that meeting. I don't have to take everything that's contained in that book as an authentic fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. So your answer is you did not mention that paragraph in your report. Yes or no, sir.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: That part of the book, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Since, sir, you have questioned certain parts of the book, apparently, let us talk about some of those camps. Are you aware, sir, that three guards or commanders from the Keraterm camp have pled guilty in the fall of 2001 and have admitted their involvement in the persecution of non-Serbs at that Keraterm camp, just like they said in the Silber book, including murder, torture, sexual assault, confinement in inhumane conditions, harassment, humiliation, and psychological abuse? And the case is Sikirica, Dosen, and Kolundzija. Are you aware that those people have pled guilty to committing those crimes at the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, but I'm not disputing the fact that there were atrocities committed on both sides, and not only in the camps that you are mentioning, but in the wider area of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, let's continue in those camps, since you questioned the Silber book, are you aware that Dusko Tadic, known as Dule, was convicted in 1997 for crimes relating to the Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje prison camps? Were you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I have to repeat once again that we don't need to mention specific admissions of guilt. I have knowledge, regardless of those admissions, that there were crimes committed on Muslim side, on the Serb side, and on all other sides. I know about that, and there were crimes committed in Sarajevo as well. I lived in Sarajevo at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But sir, you didn't say that in paragraph 70. You said: Alleged atrocities. And you said: Flimsy evidence. Which we know isn't true, that those atrocities did occur at those camps; correct? You're admitting that those atrocities have occurred at those camps.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In fact, even closer to Bosanski Samac is Brcko, which is right at the edge of the Posavina corridor; correct, sir? And in Brcko Goran Jelisic, known as the Serbian Adolf, after Adolf Hitler, pled guilty in October 1998 to serious crimes against non-civilians in the Luka camp, including 13 murders, beatings, and plunder. Were you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see why you are putting forth these examples of crimes to me when I've already said that I'm aware that there were crimes committed in Bosnia-Herzegovina by all three sides. You are now using specific examples to support my general claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at that general claim. Based on these admissions of guilt that you've just heard, which occurred in this courthouse, the decision in the Tadic case and the statement in the Silber and Little book, would you like to amend your report as to the phrase "alleged atrocities" and flimsy evidence? Would you like to amend your report at this time, sir?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: It is said here that Serb atrocities were exaggerated, that Serbs were demonised and were portrayed in an even worse light. This is what it says here, that this is how they were portrayed in Western media, and that the journalists competed among themselves as to how they were going to portray Serbs, claiming that Serbs ran extermination camps. This is what I said here. Those were not exterminating camps. Those were not Nazi camps. And I simply said that they were portrayed in an even worse light.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, you say that these weren't extermination camps. I'd like to show you a piece of evidence from the Jelisic case of the Serbian Adolf, Goran Jelisic, executing a man. And would you please look at this picture?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Expert witness already explained that he is not challenging that there were crimes, and we really don't see what is the relevance of producing one particular crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm asking him if he will change his testimony. He won't answer my question. Maybe when he sees an execution, he'll -- maybe that will affect his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would you look at that picture, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution will go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Once again, based on the evidence you've heard so far, as well as the picture of an execution right in front of you, would you change your testimony in relation to the phrases "alleged atrocities" and "flimsy evidence"? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, objection. This witness cannot say who is on that picture. There is not enough evidences that he can make any comments. I think this witness clearly stated that all three sides in Bosnia committed various war crimes. So let's be -- otherwise we are opening another case into our case with this bunch of evidence and all other photographs. He doesn't know where -- who is on that picture, et cetera. I mean, what is the sense of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution have a point which they're trying to make in relation to the expert report which is before us, so they will go ahead. Let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: If you will allow me, if you're not going to interrupt me, then I will proceed and say two sentences. Please do not interrupt me. I lived in Sarajevo during a portion of the war. There were crimes committed against Serb civilians there, and I did not need photographs to learn of this. I was there and I saw that directly. Those were crimes committed against Serb civilians. Please allow me to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: On re-direct, your counsel has the right to bring out any explanation of any answer if you feel you want further explanation. My question to you is: Are you willing to amend your report at this time? It's a yes or no. I'm not asking you about atrocities committed against Serbs, atrocities committed against Croats. I'm asking you: Are you willing to amend the information based on the evidence that has been presented to you? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot give such a simple answer to such a complex question. We're not here on a quiz, and the topic is much more complex to allow me to answer with a yes or no. Will you allow me to proceed?
