utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. I'm asking you to answer the question. If you can't answer the question, sir, we'll move on. If you feel you can't answer the question, we'll move on. If you will not -- that's fine.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot give you a yes or no answer. The question is much too complex for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Fine, sir. Now, sir, do you believe your report to be objective?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm glad you asked this question. I gave expert opinions before as well, but this time I had in front of me the expert opinion of my colleague, Dr. Donia. I analysed his report and determined it to be quite one-sided, and I tried to supplement what was missing in that report in order to give the Trial Chamber a comprehensive insight into everything that took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, apparently you didn't understand my question. My question is a simple one. Do you believe your report to be objective? Are you saying it is, and you've gone to the other side to try to neutralise Mr. Donia, the other expert, or is your report objective? Simple question.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't want to deny what Dr. Donia said. I simply wanted to supplement it in order to give a comprehensive picture to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Fine. Let's try it again. Do you believe your report to be objective, sir? I'm not asking you about Dr. Donia. I'm just asking you if you believe your report to be objective.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I cannot give you the kind of answer that you're looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I've already given you an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, in your report, you are very critical of Alija Izetbegovic. Would you please show us where in your report you criticise Radovan Karadzic, Biljana Plavsic, Slobodan Milosevic, all alleged war criminals? Please show us in your report where you criticise them.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will repeat something that I've already said. The report of Dr. Donia speaks in detail about the culpability of persons that you've just mentioned, but doesn't speak about Alija Izetbegovic and his culpability in that situation. I tried to supplement that picture precisely because Dr. Donia does not speak of it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So basically, sir, what you're saying to me is nowhere in your report do you criticise the Serb leadership, or the SDA leadership?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I've just given you an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you criticise the Serb leadership or SDS leadership in your report, sir?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I've already replied to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let us continue looking at that report. In your report, sir, you mention the pre-war preparations of the Muslims and the Croats. At paragraphs 33, 39, and 68. Where in your report do you describe the pre-war preparations of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Pre-war preparations of Bosnian Serbs were actually not necessary, if I can put it that way, because, conditionally speaking, the Serb side, or the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina, were in favour of Bosnia and Herzegovina remaining within Yugoslavia, so they didn't want the situation to change. They didn't support the changes, because they wanted Bosnia and Herzegovina to remain within Yugoslavia. This is why they believed that the Yugoslav People's Army represented the force that would defend the status quo, and this is why they probably believed that there was no particular need for them to arm themselves, because there was a regular army that was going to protect the status quo, because it was its duty, as defined by the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you saying, sir, that there were no pre-war preparations by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of any such thing. They relied upon the Yugoslav People's Army as an armed force that protects the political interests of the Bosnian Serbs, and that was the survival of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you didn't say that in your report, that the Serbs did not prepare; rather, they relied upon the Yugoslavian army. You didn't say that in your report, did you, sir?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, in my report I did not say a great many things I could have said. But if you are interested in any of that, you can put questions to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Once again, you didn't say it? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I have to tell you, quite simply, that the subject is too complex, to delicate, and if at all possible, please do not suggest that I should give simplified answers by way of yes or no only.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at some factual issues. Were you aware that the paramilitary office, paramilitary soldiers from Serbia entered the area of Bosanski Samac prior to the war which began on April 17th, 1992? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is in Donia's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you discuss that in your report?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I repeat once again. I do apologise to the Trial Chamber and everybody else for having to engage in such repetition. I wrote expert reports earlier for The Hague Tribunal too that were far more comprehensive. They included a great many facts of this nature, such as those that the Prosecutor has been referring to now. However, I had been acquainted with the expert report of my colleague, Dr. Donia, and I saw that he had quite thoroughly dealt with many of the questions that the Prosecutor is insisting upon now. Therefore, in my analysis, I dwelled on those matters that he omitted, and I thought that that was the point of expert opinions, that the Trial Chamber should be provided with as comprehensive a picture as possible as to what was going on on the ground. Quite simply, I believe that the Trial Chamber will take into account what Dr. Donia presented in his expertise, as well as that which I presented in my report. I am not entering a polemic with him in my text. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you discuss in your report the arrival of the paramilitaries in Bosanski Samac? Simple question. Did you discuss it in your report? Not your reasoning, not your basis why you did, why you didn't. Did you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, I cannot give an answer that way. I think that I have sufficiently dealt with it in my previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You still haven't answered the question. Let's move on to another question concerning this less comprehensive report. Did you indicate that local Serbs were sent to Serbia two, three months prior to the war for paramilitary training, 20 to 30 local Serbs from Bosanski Samac? Did you mention that in your report as part of the pre-war preparation?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Quite simply, I'm not aware of that particular fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. Sir, you indicate that certain --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I'm not sure that Donia mentions that fact either. Perhaps I do not remember. Perhaps it is there. But I do not recall that. However, I fully trust it, if my colleague put it in his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in your report, you mention that there were certain Muslim or Croatian barricades or checkpoints. Were you aware that the JNA and the Serbs had set up barricades and checkpoints in the municipality of Bosanski Samac prior to the war? Are you aware of that? It wasn't in your report, so that's why I'm asking the question. Are you aware of it and you deleted it, or it's not in your report and you're not aware of it? Did you not know of it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. As for the existence of Serb barricades, I know about that, but not about Samac. I know that this had existed in Sarajevo and that the army of BH, or rather the JNA, together with the police of Bosnia-Herzegovina, together with the presidency, intervened and that the barricades were removed. So I do know of Serb barricades in Sarajevo, but I do not know of barricades in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You had no mention that at least a month prior to the war JNA tanks, mortars, and artillery had been brought into that area, into the municipality of Bosanski Samac. Were you aware of it, sir, or did you know of it and decide to delete the information, not place the information in the report, or were you not aware of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do have to object to this question of the Prosecution. Maybe if our learned colleague could explain what is the basis of this statement that a month prior to the outbreak of conflict tanks and mortars and other artillery was placed in Bosanski Samac. On what basis he states that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Certainly. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in paragraph 38, going into 39 -- actually, beginning in paragraph 37, those two and a half paragraphs are the only paragraphs in this 117-page report relating to Bosanski Samac. And in the third paragraph, which would be paragraph 39, he describes factor after factor of incidents, if you want to call them, or incident after incident or action and action taken by either the Croats or the Muslims from Bosanski Samac. However, he doesn't describe any actions taken by the Serbs, and I'm asking him about this omission. He might not be aware of it. That might be the issue. It might be a lack of knowledge, or he might have deleted it for some reason and established a bias or a nonobjective or an unobjective report. And I don't know which he has done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is quite clear for the Defence what the Prosecution would like to establish through his line of cross-examination, but -- well, first, to be honest, we did not intervene when the Prosecution asked about paramilitaries. We did not intervene about sending some citizen from Bosanski Samac to a special military education. But now we are intervening, because the fact that tanks and mortars and artillery was placed, we are asking what is the basis for this statement. And we still didn't get the answer from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, when I am doing is proving that the Serbs took several actions to prepare for war, that he did not include any of those actions taken in preparation for war. So either he purposely deleted them or he just doesn't have the knowledge, he was unaware of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Because the report to some extent goes into factual matters in the sense that, as the Prosecution is putting it, he describes what the other people were doing, the Croats and the Muslims, and as Mr. Weiner has said, he's trying to find out whether his report could have been balanced in giving information on what the Serbs were also doing. So the Prosecution can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that JNA tanks, mortars, and artillery were brought into the area or the municipality of Bosanski Samac around March of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: In order to clarify this, are you referring to JNA artillery or some other Serb forces, paramilitary forces, or are you talking about JNA artillery?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: JNA artillery. Artillery, tanks, or mortars that had never been in that area before suddenly arrives approximately one and a half months prior to the war. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, I didn't know that. But I don't see anything controversial about this. The JNA was the regular army of that country, and there was nothing strange about it or suspicious about it if army units were moving about in a country where there are regular military force, especially when the situation was particularly difficult. Because incidents had already started. There was unrest. And it is normal that military and police forces should be present and should be moving about, of course, in a way which their commands consider to be the proper way to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You said that there was nothing strange about it. The fact that mortars are now facing the non-Serb towns, artillery is facing the non-Serb towns, and tanks that have never been seen in that area suddenly appear, that's not strange to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Again I have to object.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's argumentative. I'll withdraw. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned the new TO. Were you aware that Serbs were invited to join the new TO, or Territorial Defence, of Bosanski Samac? Were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that specifically, but I have to tell you in general terms that in my expert report I have been dealing with the situation in general, as you also noticed in extensive text, I only refer to Samac in three paragraphs, and the text is about 100 pages. So I'm dealing with the general situation, and therefore I wish to remind you that there were also Muslims and Croats involved, that they were called up in accordance with the law. They were called up as conscripts. However, there was a sabotage and they refused to go along with this legal obligation of theirs. The TO --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, we're talking about the TO of Bosanski Samac, not the other TOs in the country, not the draft. Were you aware that Serbs were invited to join the Territorial Defence of -- the new Territorial Defence of Bosanski Samac? Were you aware of that in April of 1992, the Serb civilians were invited to join?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Specifically, as far as Bosanski Samac is concerned, I don't know. I cannot really say anything to you. I can only say what the situation was generally in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. And in fairness to this witness, Mr. Weiner, I think it's clear now that he has explained that he was describing the situation in general, so he has no particular details of any particular place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you have no knowledge of what happened in April of 1992, April and May of 1992, in Bosanski Samac, sir; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when you're talking about concrete things in Bosanski Samac, there is nothing that I can confirm or deny. I can only tell you in principle what the situation was with the Yugoslav People's Army in Bosnia-Herzegovina, also as regards the TO, et cetera, and I can refer only in the barest terms to the situation in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So obviously, I'll take it the next step - you weren't aware of the prison camps or the detention centres that were established in Bosanski Samac in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. In that respect, I know what the situation was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you a few more questions about the area. In your report, at paragraph 64, you mention an attack on Bosanski Brod. You mention, actually, a massacre of Serbs in Bosanski Brod.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: What paragraph was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 64, sir.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: This has to do with the massacre in the village of Sijekovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, sir, did you, in your report, mention at that same time period the attack on Bijeljina by Serb paramilitaries? Did you mention that, sir, where they had summary executions in the street of Muslim political leaders? Did you mention that in your report, the attack on Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: In my previous expert reports, I mentioned both. However, as I said a minute ago, this was extensively dealt with in Dr. Donia's expertise, whereas Sijekovac was not mentioned. Both cases occurred within a short span of time, and the members of the presidency were Fikret Abdic, Biljana Plavsic, Franjo Boras, and they went to both places and both tragic incidents attracted a great deal of attention at the time. This was the beginning of such developments in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Since you mentioned this in your other reports, which I apologise I haven't seen, would you agree that in a period of one week, on April 1st, the Serb paramilitaries, Arkan's paramilitaries, attacked Bijeljina, and on April 8th, one week later, the paramilitaries attacked Zvornik, and in both cases there were summary executions in the street, thousands of people lost their homes, people were beaten? Do you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Once again, I have to repeat my general statement that crimes were committed in that period both against Bosniaks and Croats and Serbs, in different parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was an immediate eyewitness of this in Sarajevo. As I said a minute ago, I was aware of the tragic events in Bijeljina. You yourself confirmed the tragic events in Sijekovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about Sarajevo. I'm asking you about two particular places just east of Bosanski Samac: Bijeljina and Zvornik. Are you aware of those specific atrocities occurring? They weren't listed in your report. Are you aware that they occurred? I'm not asking about Sarajevo. I'm not asking about other atrocities. We could stay here for days talking about every atrocities. Those two. Are you aware of those two, one on April 1st and one on April 8th?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I have confirmed to you these crimes in Bijeljina. I don't see why you're asking me about that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Bijeljina is fine. What about Zvornik, one week later on April 8th?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I do not recall. These crimes later became a mass phenomenon in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Bijeljina and Sijekovac, though, I remember very well, because that was the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, let's move on. You mention in your report, in your criticism of Alija Izetbegovic, his goal, or what you believe to be his interest in establishing a united Muslim community or a pan-Muslim nation, or something along those lines. You never in your report mention the goal of a greater Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the interest of the wish of Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina was no Greater Serbia. Rather, it was the preservation of Great Yugoslavia. The plebiscite that was held in Bosnia-Herzegovina before the referendum, if you remember, the question in it was not the question at the referendum that was organised by the Serb Democratic Party was not: Are you in favour of a Greater Serbia or not, but the question was: Are you in favour of preserving Yugoslavia or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, even though you make that statement that the Serbs weren't interested in a Greater Serbia, are you aware that in the case of Prosecutor versus Dusko Tadic, also known as Dule, in the decision, the Court states the following, paragraph 85: "The concept of a Greater Serbia has a long history. It emerged at the forefront of political consciousness, close to its modern-day form. As early as 150 years ago and gained momentum between the two world wars, kept in check during the years of Marshal Tito's rule, it became very active after his death. Greater Serbia involved two distinct aspects. First, the incorporation of two autonomous provinces of Vojvodina and Kosovo into Serbia, already referred to; and secondly, the extension of the enlarged Serbia, together with Montenegro, into portions of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, containing substantial Serb populations." Were you aware of that quote and that information from the Dusko Tadic decision?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. But what I am aware of is, since we're talking about awareness, tradition, et cetera, and of course this is not the subject of this discussion here, what kind of plans or ideas were espoused by individual politicians anywhere, including Serbia and Belgrade. But as for politicians in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was an unequivocal option in favour of Yugoslavia, and therefore, the question at the plebiscite was worded the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about politicians.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Allow me to finish, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, you're not answering my question, sir. You have to answer the questions. So let's talk about the politicians of Bosnia. I'll take the portion from your answer. Paragraph 89: "In the early 1990s there were rallies that advocated and promoted the idea with Serbian leaders in attendance. In 1992, Radoslav Brdjanin, president of the Crisis Staff of the Serb autonomous region of Banja Luka area, declared that 2 per cent was the upper --"

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is not clear to me. Which document are you quoting from?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The Tadic decision. He "declared that 2 per cent was the upper tolerable limit on the presence of all non-Serbs in the region. Radoslav Brdjanin advocated three stages of ridding the area of non-Serbs. 1, creating impossible conditions that would have the effect of encouraging them to leave of their own accord, involving pressure and terror tactics; 2, deportation and banishment; and 3, liquidating those remaining who would not fit into his concept for the region." Are you aware of Radoslav Brdjanin making those particular comments or any other rallies in Bosnia-Herzegovina where the concept of Greater Serbia was discussed?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can I just put a question to you for the sake of clarification and accuracy?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Certainly, sir.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now put your question to me? What is your question on the basis of all of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of that comment or similar comments by any SDS or Serb party politicians?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what people -- officials of the SDS spoke individually at lower levels. However, their leaders, people who held top offices in the SDS in Republika Srpska, I don't know of them having made such statements that they want to create a Greater Serbia. I never heard about that, for one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, you are aware that your time is almost up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I just have one more area after this. He's not answering the questions, Your Honour, and he goes on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That sometimes happens. So you simply make your point and you move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: One more quotation and then we'll move on to the last topic, sir. Sir, are you aware -- you mentioned -- and the reason I'm asking this you mentioned in one sentence the Serb autonomous regions in your report, just one sentence. But are you aware of the tie between the Greater Serbia theory and the Serb autonomous regions. And this I'm quoting from, again, the Tadic decision, paragraph 97: "The greater Serbia theory was put into practice after the 1990 elections and before the beginning of the war. In April of 1991, several communities joined a Serbian association of municipalities --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speaker please slow down. The reading is too fast for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: "In April 1991, several communities joined a Serbian association of municipalities. These structures were formed in areas predominantly inhabited by Bosnian Serbs, generally by vote of the predominantly Bosnian Serb local assemblies. At first, this association was a form of economic and cultural cooperation with administrative power. However, separate police forces and separate assemblies rapidly developed. In September 1991, it was announced that several Serb autonomous regions in Bosnia and Herzegovina had been proclaimed, including the Krajina, Romanija, Stara Hercegovina, with the aim of separating the republican government agencies in Sarajevo and creating a Greater Serbia." Had you ever heard that information before, sir?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, listen. These are topics that are dealt with in the expert opinion, expert report, and I can give you specific answers regarding them because they have to do with the global political movements. What I believe is that these autonomous regions, these so-called SAOs, the Serbian autonomous regions, and if I understood your question well, you asked me whether I see a link between that and Greater Serbia. However, I see a different kind of link there between these autonomous regions, on the one hand, and on the other hand, what -- during the peace negotiations up until Dayton was discussed, namely, how to decentralise Bosnia-Herzegovina along the lines of the ethnical principle, because three sides participated in negotiations. There is something that was the established structure in Bosnia and Herzegovina regarding decentralisation and regionalisation, namely, that western Herzegovina was mostly populated by Croats, Cazin area was mostly populated by Muslims and then certain other areas were mostly populated by Serbs, and so on. It is true though, that some areas had mixed population, ethnically mixed population. The Croatian of these autonomous regions, and not only Serb ones but also Croat ones, which you know existed. There was the western Herzegovina as a region, and so on. So let me just conclude --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Just conclude.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, I do not see a link there. I don't see how this is linked to the concept of Greater Serbia. But if you insist, the link that I see has to do with a decentralised Bosnia-Herzegovina, which through all of these arrangements, starting with Lisbon and all the way up to Dayton, was discussed, and in a sense it represents a continuation of the previous state that I've described. Naturally, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. Excuse me, Mr. Kecmanovic. Intervention -- correction to the transcript. Page 62, line 3. I think that the professor mentioned, after the Croatian region of Herceg-Bosna, and then he mentioned Croatian region of Bosanska Posavina. He said that, but we don't have that in transcript. Maybe my learned friend can clarify that or simply I can do that in re-direct, whatever is suitable. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Re-direct would probably be better, because it's not in answer to my question anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicate -- last question on this. You indicate that you understand the concept of Greater Serbia. You never mention in your report, in your 117-plus-paragraph report, the concept of Greater Serbia in your -- in this report, sir; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Once again, I need a clarification. You said that I understood, grasped the concept. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the concept of Greater Serbia. Those are your words. And you talk about the concept of Greater Serbia. And my question is: You never mention it in your 60-page report; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't believe it to be relevant to the events in Bosnia. I will repeat this again. Bosnian Serbs did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... whether you agree it to be relevant or not, you never mention it; is that correct? Can you agree with me that you never mentioned the concept of Greater Serbia in your 60-page report? Whether you -- regardless of your views on its relevance, you never mention it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: This concept was not mentioned anywhere by the leaders of the SDS either, or leaders of Serbian Republic, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But I'm not asking you that question, because we can get into that if we had more time. You never mention it in your 60-page report, sir; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go on to one final issue. As you know -- or I believe you know the defendants in this case have been charged with ethnic cleansing, to wit, crimes of transfer of civilians, deportation. In your 60-page report, you never mention ethnic cleansing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We already have this kind of questions during testimonies of witnesses and other expert witnesses of the Prosecution, when we asked those kind of witnesses, even expert witnesses, about ethnic cleansing. We have to understand that it's a legal term. And as our learned colleague said, this witness has no legal education.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the phrases deportation, transfer, have legal meanings. Ethnic cleansing is a common term which was used by the newspapers, the press, the politicians, the diplomats --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I mean, to be brief, why don't you just explain what your question is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: My question, sir, is: You never mentioned the term or the phrase "ethnic cleansing" in your report; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I can once again give an answer, but not a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the term "ethnic cleansing" refers to? If you don't let me give you that first. Ethnic cleansing, according to the Special Rapporteur of the UN Commission on Human Rights for Yugoslavia on 28 August 1992 states: "Ethnic cleansing refers to the elimination by the ethnic group exercising control over a given territory of members of other ethnic groups." Do you discuss in any place in your 60-page report the concept of ethnic cleansing or the ethnic cleansing which occurred in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the war?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: If you want me to give a yes or no answer, I will then exercise my right not to give you an answer, because I would like to answer in one or two sentences. I cannot simply answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, the question is: Does it exist in your report or doesn't it exist in your report? On re-direct examination, you can explain why you placed it there or why you didn't place it there. Do you agree with me, though, it does not exist in your 60-page report?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, listen. Then my answer is not really important there. We can simply go through the report and see whether it's mentioned there or not. This is simply a matter of record. We can go through the text and see whether it's mentioned in the text or not. It's not relevant what I'm going to say. If you want me to give an explanation about why is that not mentioned in my report, then I can do that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you are agreeing that it is not mentioned in your report, then?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Final question. Sir, are you aware of the decision on strategic objectives of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina? It was drafted on 12 May 1992, and strategic objective number 1 and this is an exhibit which is in evidence in this case. Strategic objective number 1 is to establish state borders separating the Serbian people from the other two ethnic communities, and that was drafted on 12 May 1992 by Momcilo Krajisnik, president of the National Assembly. Are you aware of that document?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And are you aware -- were you aware that that document was adopted by the Republic of Srpska assembly?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that? I didn't quite understand the bit that had to do with state borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I can be of some assistance. If the document can be shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's Prosecution Exhibit P5?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I invite your attention to Article 1, please.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of that document and familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Not in detail, but please put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All my question was, since we're talking about ethnic cleansing: Were you aware of this decision which was adopted by the Republika Srpska Assembly? And it's number 1 was to establish state borders separating the Serbian people from the other two ethnic communities, and it was signed by President -- or stamped by President of the National Assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Where does it talk about state borders?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Article 1 says: "The strategic objectives or priorities of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina are to: 1. Establish state borders separating the Serbian people from the other two ethnic communities."

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And it comes from a session held on 12 May 1992 of the assembly of Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You're aware of that. Last question --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I just learned of that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were never aware of this document prior to -- or that vote prior to today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the fact that my colleague from the Prosecution mentioned the date of this document, and we have dealt with this before with this Trial Chamber, since this witness at the time was not a member of the assembly, could we please hear when was this decision announced in the Official Gazette, not when it was adopted, but when was it announced or published. Because I think that the publishing date was one year later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, do you have that information?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, I don't. I have the English translation. It's not there. I'm just trying to determine if he was aware of it, being an expert on political affairs. Because it's not in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So you don't know when it was established? So you just want to find out whether the witness was aware of this decision. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, this decision. He has the gazette right there. He can probably tell us from the front page the date of its publication.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 26th of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you aware of that, or is today the first day that you've become aware of that decision?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the first time that I see it in the original form.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Had you been made aware of the objectives, even though you haven't seen it in the original form? Were you aware of those objectives and those statements, those six statements or objectives listed there?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not in this specific concrete form, but regarding this, I can only tell you that these objectives -- may I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: All I can say is that these objectives changed based on the situation. We had a plebiscite where Serbs opted for remaining in Yugoslavia. Then in Lisbon, Bosnia-Herzegovina was accepted as a decentralised state, which is a completely different concept and then we have this that you're bringing up. After this the Serb signed the Dayton Accords and it's a completely different matter with respect to the previous one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, please wind up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: One last question, sir. You indicated that you read Professor Donia or Dr. Donia's report. He mentions the variant A and B document. Were you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I have heard of it, but I don't know any specific details regarding it. I've heard of it recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Professor, we need to conclude before the break. My first question during re-direct stems from the question put to you by the Prosecutor. While preparing a scientific report, an academic report, so when preparing an expert opinion, an expert report, could you please explain the method that you use when preparing such reports, expert reports. What is your method when writing scholarly papers?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, when you're writing scholarly works, how do you define your sources? How do you formulate them? How do you deduce conclusions? Can you please describe your methodology for us.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: If this has to do with the question put to me by the Prosecutor, then I have to say that no report, especially such a brief one, can take into account all facts and all sources. One has to make a selection, and in compressing this, I had to -- I counted on the discussion that we will have here before the Trial Chamber, where I will be given an opportunity to give explanations and so on. However, Mr. Prosecutor, by limiting my answers, did not allow me to proceed with that, and I think that the Trial Chamber thus was denied further explanations which would be quite useful in creating the comprehensive picture that would complement what Dr. Donia stated in his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Pantelic. Just for the sake of clarity, is my understanding of your question correct when you're talking about researching a scholarly work, were you referring to the issue of how you research UN documents, whether you cite primary sources, whether you rely on newspaper articles in lieu of such, or was your question directed to something broader than that? I'm just a bit uncertain.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My -- that is the gist of my question. The process how one will prepare his report in process of citing and stuff like that, yes. But of course including this part of answer, which is quite logical. Otherwise the report can be thousands of pages maybe. Thank you, Your Honour, for your intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you spoke about a certain domination of the Croat and Muslim political parties which dominated the political life, the parliament, and the presidency. I would like to ask you this now, whether this domination of the Croat/Muslim coalition transferred to other regions in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the time period relevant and described in your report.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those were central organs of government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that was the centre of political life in Bosnia. It is quite natural for every country, including Bosnia and Herzegovina, to have events that transpire in capital to other areas, and therefore these events had their reflection elsewhere in Bosnia. Political conflicts that broke out in the parliament, outvoting and so on, yes, they had direct repercussions in other regions. Political conflicts broke out in Sarajevo, whereas violent conflicts emerged in the provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So based on this coalition that was established, you say that these relations transferred or spread to other areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If you have in mind the symmetry that I spoke about with ratio 2:1, then it went, it flowed from upper levels to lower levels along the political party structure. Even before the elections, the conflict became apparent, and especially once the third party entered the conflict, then this basically spread out down the municipal structure. So one aspect of it was the government, where there was a confrontation, and then it also had its effects in the political parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You participated in the political life in Bosnia-Herzegovina after the multiparty elections in 1990. In view of the fact that you were born in Bosnia, did you in that capacity, as a politician, as a scholar, as a publicist have you ever in that capacity visited Samac afterwards and do you have information or knowledge about the events, local events, in Samac? Were you interested in that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I have to say that my knowledge about Samac is quite limited, and as I've already stated, I mostly limited myself to the general picture of the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And this thesis of mine is that this global picture had its reflections in provinces. So I did travel to Bosanski Samac. I visited that place. The party that I was a member of had its branch offices in Bosanski Samac, and I travelled to that town, especially in a post-war period. On my way to Banja Luka I would stop in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Another question of mine that stemmed from the question put by the Prosecutor. You mentioned a massacre of Serbs in Sijekovac, which is quite near Bosanski Samac. What is your opinion? Did this tragic event have any effects in Posavina and in Samac, in view of a very tense political situation? What is your opinion of this?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: The event in Sijekovac, as I've already stated, was one of the first large incidents that caused great number of victims, and once the war broke out, there were a lot of victims everywhere. But at that time, there was still peace. And yes, that event had very serious effects in the whole of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My next question is that you were -- since you were a member of the party of reformist forces, was the SDS, in a political sense, your opponent?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not only among the members of the reformist party, but also among those members of the SDP. We kept a certain distance from all three national parties. And yes, in the political sense, yes, they were our opponents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We have to correct the transcript. If I am not mistaken, you said that Croats in Bosnia created their regions. You mentioned western Herzegovina and also Posavina. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And this came about immediately after the HDZ expressed its support of creating independent Bosnia, because the HDZ opted for supporting the establishment of independent Bosnia and Herzegovina. Those Croats who in the elections voted mostly for the HDZ followed this in the referendum, but despite that, shortly after the referendum, the creation of the so-called HAOs was begun, meaning Croatian autonomous regions. These were areas that were predominantly populated by Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Later on, in confrontations after Dayton, when the third entity was discussed, members of the HDZ explained this ambivalent position in the following way: They said that in the referendum, they supported the wholesomeness of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state, but at the time they did not touch upon its internal structure and that they believed that question should be dealt with later on, and this is how they tried to get through the door the discussion about the creation of the third entity that would be representing Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. When I say "Croats," I'm referring to regions that are predominantly populated by Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In that context, can you tell us what was controlled by the Muslim leadership? You've just touched upon this sphere of interests of the Croat and the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in a way, this was a Bosnia-Herzegovina consisting of three entities. There were three separate national units, and what created the confusion was that the Serbs and Croats, with their national leadership, defined their territories and their administration clearly, as Croat or Serb territories in Bosnia, whereas the Muslim side, during that entire period, declared what was the Muslim administration as the Bosnian administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I didn't want to interrupt the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: An objection or I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I gave them the benefit when they talked about Croat-controlled areas, which was outside of cross-examination. Now they're into Muslim-controlled areas, which is well outside cross-examination. This isn't re-direct. This is trying to get in what they couldn't get in on direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This is just to cover the illustration and last question with regard to variant A and B and I'm finished, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Professor, when the Prosecutor asked you about variant A and B, you told us that you had just learned about that recently. From what source? Books, the media? How did you learn of this variant A and B?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that I came upon that in Dr. Donia's report. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I don't have further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor Kecmanovic, for giving evidence to the Trial Chamber. You are now finished. You can leave the courtroom and you can also go. Yes. It's actually just after 1300 hours and the Trial Chamber will rise and we'll sit this afternoon from 1430 hours. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.03 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Please be seated. Who will examine the witness? Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you hear the interpretation all right?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes everything is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We should speak at a slower pace in order to give the interpreters an opportunity to translate this, and I would ask you to make a pause --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: One of our microphones is not working for Judge Williams. Can somebody from the machine room help us? It's not picking up channel 4. Judge Williams's microphone. Maybe we can test. Can the interpreters say something?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the interpreters now? Can you hear channel 4?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We can proceed, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, Professor, due to technical considerations that I told you about, we should make a pause between question and answer so that we are assured that both the questions and answers will be recorded in the transcript. We know that you arrived just yesterday, and in view of your advanced age, please let us know if you should feel any discomfort or fatigue, so that we know about it and then the Trial Chamber will be able to do something regarding that. Professor, in your expert opinion, you dealt with constitutional aspects in quite a great detail. In view of the instructions of the Trial Chamber, we will not go into further explanations of some portions of your expert opinion. Therefore, I will ask you just a few questions regarding your professional and personal biography. First of all, as we analysed your resume, your curriculum vitae, you told me that the book that you published in Italy - and this can be found at page 2 of your curriculum vitae -- it is recorded in your c.v. that this book was published when in fact --

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. In fact it was published in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Professor, please tell us: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was born in Belgrade on the 23rd of April, 1928.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: During your schooling and during your life in the post-war period, you were known as a person who was -- who had an anti-regime or an anti-communist attitude; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, especially after the beginning of dictatorship of Slobodan Milosevic. During the previous time, I had a critical view of the Tito's communist regime; however, no significant consequences ensued as a result of that viewpoint of mine. However, from the beginning, I did have some repercussions in that I was not immediately elected to my post at the faculty, the post of assistant professor, due to my political views. However, later on I was elected to that post. In the dictatorship regime of Slobodan Milosevic, without any false modesty, I can say that as far as the constitutional viewpoint is concerned, I was one of the greatest critics of his constitution of Serbia from 1993 and the federal constitution of Yugoslavia from 1992. I was also a critic of a number of his acts that I qualified as unconstitutional, criminal, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: During your schooling and specialist training, you also spent some time abroad, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I received a scholarship from the French government as a result of which I spent the entire school year in France, cooperating with the then most important professor of constitutional law, Georges Videl [phoen] from the Sorbonne university. I would like to add that prior to that, as a young assistant professor, I applied for the Ford scholarship in the United States. However, I did not receive an approval from the Yugoslav committee in charge of that, so the American committee never had an opportunity to review my application. I spent some time in France, not only on the occasion that I described to you, but later on, during some additional training that I received, and I also lectured at the Sorbonne university.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The reason you gave for your failure to receive the American Ford scholarship is connected with a certain communist political structures which did not support you in your bid to go to America for specialisation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It was mostly people favoured by the regime who were approved by the authorities who received such scholarships.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Regardless of this, you were an honourary professor of Columbia University, a French university in Rouen, and also at the Sorbonne. You lectured in Fribourg in Switzerland; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This is correct, but I have to clarify. The doctor honoris causa was awarded to me at the French university of Rouen, in Bogota in Columbia. They do not give honourary doctorates. So I was elected an honourary professor. At the Sorbonne, however, the Pantheon Sorbonne in Paris one, I was also a professor. At Fribourg I was invited to give lectures as a professor, and I have also given lectures at over 40 universities worldwide. So in all, I held 50 or 60 courses of lectures, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Another question and then we will finish with this topic. You are also one of the founders of the international association for constitutional law; is that correct? Who were your colleagues who were cofounders of this association?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The international association for constitutional law was founded in 1981 on the initiative of a professor from Argentina, and also professors from France, and some other countries, and it was decided that the establishing of this international association, which today encompasses over 40 national organisations, should take place in Belgrade. On that occasion, a founding assembly was convened, at which there were several professors from Belgrade, including me, as well as professors from France, Greece, Switzerland, and a number of other countries. Today the executive board consists of representatives of many countries, and I can say with pleasure that the future president of this international organisation will be our esteemed colleague from Australia, Cheryl Saunders [phoen] from Melbourne University, and today a professor from Finland, a dear colleague of ours from Turku University, professor Ante Jurankis [phoen] is the president of this association. There are some others who have been very active ever since the beginning, ever since the founding of this association.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You were the Secretary-General of this association from 1993 and you are also one of the vice-presidents of this association; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My last question: You are also a member of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. There is some inconsistency in the transcript. The question was -- posed to the witness, and I heard it from our colleague Pantelic: You were the Secretary-General of this association until 1993, not from 1993. It makes a difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will clarify that, if you will allow me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is a matter of the transcript --

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: From 1981, when the association was established, it was right away that I was elected Secretary-General, and I remained at that post until 1993, when I resigned because Yugoslavia was then -- the sanctions had been imposed on Yugoslavia, so I was unable to contact the other national associations, especially as regarded financial matters. The Executive Council of the international organisation accepted my resignation, and right away they elected me vice-president, and I'm still in that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One last question in connection with your membership of the crown council, could you please explain what kind of council this is and what your function in it is?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this question, because it gives me an opportunity, not wanting to take up the time of the Trial Chamber and the others present here. Serbia, throughout its historical development, was a monarchy. It was only under the communist regime of Tito and the communist dictatorship of Slobodan Milosevic that it became a republic. The consequences of this fateful revolutionary transformation are still felt today. The son of the last king, King Peter the 2nd, who died abroad as a refugee, as were the other members of the dynasty, returned to the country after the radical transformation that took place on the 5th of October, 2002. But even some ten years before that, he was active in promoting the welfare of the Serbian people. And in connection with this, he established a crown council. This is an advisory body advising the crown, the heir to the thrown, and the aim of this council is to communicate with him and to give him their opinions, their proposals, and initiatives. That is the reason why the crown council was set up. And I was one of the first five or six members of this council, and I was elected to it in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. We shall now discuss your work. Only a few questions, in view of the time we have at our disposal. Tell me, please: What is your professional standpoint in relation to the fact that in the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which consists of representatives of the three constituent peoples, in October 1991, the Serbian people were outvoted by the Croatian and Muslim people, and what were the consequences of this in the constitutional sense, since you discussed this in your paper?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote a few pages about this, but with Their Honours' leave and the leave of the Prosecutors, I would only like to emphasise some things. Bosnia and Herzegovina was established as a federal unit in the period just after the end of World War II, but in essence, this was an artificial construct. There were three constituent nations on its territory. The Croatian, Serbian, and Muslim people. In the beginning, the Muslims did not have the status of a constituent people, but Tito's communist regime gave them this status in the 1970s, so that still today they are a constituent nation, and this is a fait accompli. The other federal units in federal socialist Yugoslavia were established on the national principle. The Croats had Croatia, the Serbs had Serbia, the Montenegrins had Montenegro, and so on and so forth. The same goes for the Slovenes and the Macedonians. Therefore, in the case of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is of crucial importance, a problem of crucial importance is that of the equality of these three peoples and their acting on the principle of consensus. However, in the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, certain tendencies emerged, not only there, but also in the parties that were established on the -- on ethnic principles, and a coalition was established between the HDZ and the SDA which tended toward independence. This was in the early 1990s. They tended toward the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this coalition outvoted on several occasions the third constituent nation, that is, the Serbs, and this is ultimately the cause that led to the Serb MPs leaving the assembly. There were also other political circumstances and measures which I feel -- I believe have been discussed here which contributed to this, and this is why the Serbian deputies left and established their own assembly, but in their documents they expressed the intention of remaining in the joint assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but only to the extent that this did not go against the interests of the Serbian people. So they were going to stay in the assembly, but only provided it did not go against the interests of the Serbian people. This is all I can say now, but I would appreciate being given the opportunity to explain some matters in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The next area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to make it clear to the witness that his expert opinion report was filed with the Trial Chamber, and we all have copies of it and we have read it. So that's why we are not interested in going -- into discussing what is already on paper. And Mr. Pantelic, please do wind up, only essential areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will take care about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A second area which is of importance to the Defence is the fact that when, after the plebiscite, the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was established and adopted its constitution, bearing in mind what you have just said, can it be said that this was an illegal, illegitimate body, or was it a sort of shadow government? I'm now asking about the legality of the establishment of the assembly of Republika Srpska and the adoption of its constitution. If you could only go into this briefly and then I will have just one further question about the local level.

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Your question is doubtless one of the crucial questions in relation to the subject-matter, which requires more detailed answers. I have written quite a lot about this, but bearing in mind what Her Honour has said, I will say only the following: I am deeply convinced that the legislation passed by the Serbian deputies when they set up their own assembly and then adopted and promulgated the constitution, were absolutely legal and legitimate, legal and legitimate. I can only adduce some facts to support this. At that time, the order, not only of Yugoslavia as a federal state but also of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a federal unit, had been badly disrupted. The rights of the Serbian people were imperiled and they were in danger of becoming an ethnic minority in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is why the passing of the appropriate legislation and the adoption of the constitution on the basis of the right to self-determination, which in my view is the most important fact in this entire discussion, the assembly of the Serbian people adopted this constitution. I believe I will have an opportunity to say a little more about the right to self-determination, but for the present, I would only like to mention this fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In connection with the local assembly, the municipal assembly, can you please explain, because at that time there was no such institution as mayor in the area. All that existed was the president of the Municipal Assembly. What part did the president of the Municipal Assembly play?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This is something that was left over from the previous regime of Yugoslavia as a whole and of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a federal unit. At the local level, to be specific, at the municipal level, in accordance with the principle that was formally in force at the time - and if given the opportunity, I will explain this in greater detail - there was a principle of unity of government, and the main exponent of the government was the assembly, which had an executive organ and administrative organs. The president of the assembly was only the president of the assembly. He was not some sort of mayor or anything like that. The president of the assembly in that system - and when the constitution of Republika Srpska was adopted in 1991, this remained the same - he was only primus inter pares, the first among equals, and he had no special authority or powers. His function was mainly to convene and chair sessions of the assembly, establish an agenda, keep order at sessions, coordinate the work of various working bodies of the assembly, and so on and so forth. He did not have any powers of government. And this is what made him different from the institution of mayor. In our countries, because these are special offices in those countries, as distinct from speakers of parliaments or assemblies or other territorial units.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And my last question in connection with this topic. Briefly, the executive board, that is, the government, both at local and higher levels, and the relation between the local executive board and the structures in the ministries, how did this function, both in peacetime and in wartime? Very briefly. And where was the power actually?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As I said, this was a continuation of the system of former socialist Yugoslavia in accordance with the principle of unity of government. The executive board was an executive organ. This was called "comite," committee, from the time of the French revolution onwards. So they worked for the assembly. And in normal times, this organ supervised the administrative organs, which were set up separately. So this was an operative body which had certain powers of government within the limits of the statute, the legislation, and the constitution. However, in the period when, in 1992, the constitution of Republika Srpska was adopted, the principle of unity of government was abandoned because the constitution expressly provided for a division of power. So, however, in practice, no changes occurred. The executive organ remained, such as it was. It could be linked to administrative organs in terms of personnel, which meant that senior officials were in these organs, but in times of imminent threat of war and wartime, the situation changed radically, because in such cases the elements of decentralisation which existed under the pressure of the circumstances arising during times of imminent threat of war, they -- the various ministries acquired more direct powers in relation to local organs of administration and also partially the executive board. So that the assembly was suppressed to a large extent, which also meant that its president did not have the same powers. The government then acquired more direct powers, especially the minister of the interior, but also other ministers, such as the minister for agriculture and so on and so forth. Because everything had to be directed toward the achievement of the goals imposed by the situation of war or imminent threat of war. So that the element of centralism under these circumstances was much stronger, and therefore there was a departure from the system as it was envisaged. I wish to say that this is something that was not unique to Republika Srpska. This is something that happens in many countries. It is well known that constitutions, especially at the level of the central government, when there is a state of war or an imminent threat of war, there are much bigger powers given to the leaders of the country, the president, and the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Professor [In English] That was the end of my examination-in-chief I would say, so the witness is yours, my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the numbers for the report and the curriculum vitae. Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I had just one question -- in fact, a suggestion, if it is necessary, in view of the Trial Chamber. It has not been discussed in this expert opinion. Last year the Trial Chamber wanted to find out more about the local community, and this was not covered by this expert opinion. However, if the Trial Chamber needs to learn what the definition of the local community is and what is its relationship with other organs at other levels, then perhaps this would be a good opportunity to ask the professor to explain this. However, should the Trial Chamber not feel this is necessary, then, naturally, this will not be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Can we have the numbers first, before we forget, for the report and the c.v. The report includes the annex.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It will be D54/1 and D54A/1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. The Trial Chamber is of the view that this witness is dealing with the report which has been filed, as per rules, and we are going to proceed like that. If at any time the Trial Chamber feels that there is a need for such evidence, the Trial Chamber will call for such evidence, as provided for under the Rules. Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Professor Nikolic, my name is David Re from the Prosecution. I'm going to ask you some questions. We thank you for coming here this afternoon. The lengthy report which you've prepared and has been tendered into evidence, did you prepare this yourself or did you have research assistants help you with it?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I prepared it personally, because even before I was asked to come and appear in this case, I dealt with the subject-matter. As was mentioned in the beginning, I published a book in Italian. The Italians wanted me to write a book --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that. I was only asking you whether you prepared it yourself. The answer is yes, I take it.

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. In preparing an expert -- I withdraw that. Do you -- of course, as a constitutional expert of many years' experience, recognise and respect the opinions of constitutional courts of different countries, don't you?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course, it's one of the tools of your trade, isn't it, analysing the judgements of constitutional courts?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I have to say that in certain situations - and I have to say this with great regret - the fact that this took place in Yugoslavia, namely, that the constitutional courts passed decisions that satisfied or were in accordance with the position taken by the regime, which naturally jeopardises the dignity and reputation of the constitutional judiciary, which, as a famous French professor Louis Favere [phoen] said, represents one of the greatest achievements of the civilisation after the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Nonetheless, even if you don't agree with the decision of a constitutional court of one of the countries of the former Yugoslavia, as a constitutional lawyer, you would recognise its existence, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It is an integral part of the legal system and is carried out in accordance with the way that has been decided in that country.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you just please listen to the question I'm asking you, and I'm talking about you as a constitutional expert. I ask you whether you, as a constitutional expert, would recognise the existence of the decision.

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It is recognised because it is upheld by state organs that must implement it. However, every citizen is allowed to have its own opinion. During the dictatorship of Milosevic, I criticised decisions passed by the constitutional court on a number of occasions because they had been passed in order to suit the spirit of his regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Again, I'm asking you only about the existence of decisions and you as a constitutional expert. You recognise the fact that there are constitutional decisions of courts, don't you? It's a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And of course, as a constitutional lawyer, in preparing a report for a body such as this, and in recognising the decisions -- the fact that decisions exist, you would refer to them, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I didn't review these decisions. I simply familiarised myself with original documents that had a specific effect in reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So are you saying you've come here with a report on the constitutions of the Republic -- the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Republika Srpska, and the Socialist Republic of the former Yugoslavia -- the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, looked at those documents, the constitutional documents, but haven't looked at the decisions of the constitutional courts in relation to those documents? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. My learned friend should be more specified. I mean, we are wasting so much time with this general nature of the question. Why he simply put the question to professor: Are you familiar or are you aware of certain decision of the constitutional court of -- because we don't know yet which court, Bosnia, Austria, Italy, or whatever. So let's move on in this particular thing. That's just a suggestion with the flavour of objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think the Prosecution can be more specific so that the witness is -- the witness's mind is directed to particular decisions which maybe the Prosecution would like to discuss with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You referred to the constitutions of the three governments I referred to a moment ago without referring to any constitutional court decisions, don't you?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I did not -- I have not mentioned them, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You haven't mentioned a ruling of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- sorry, the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina constitutional court of the 1st of November, 1991, annulling the agreements to join the association of the Bosanska Krajina municipalities, have you?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I haven't mentioned it. And if you wish, I can tell you why.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You haven't mentioned the fact that the Bosnian government took the question to the constitutional court, which was the highest court in the land, have you?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You haven't mentioned in your report that the Bosnian government took that question to the constitutional court of Bosnia, have you?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Neither have you mentioned that, on the 18th of September, 1992, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina constitutional court annulled the decision on the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. You haven't mentioned that in your report either, have you?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You also haven't mentioned in your report that on the 8th of October, 1992, again the same court, the highest constitutional court in Bosnia, then an internationally recognised sovereign nation, annulled the declaration, the proclamation of the Republic of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, have you?
