utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I have not, and I would like to explain why. Putting some questions such questions at a first glance seems to be very appropriate, in view of the high reputation that the constitutional judiciary has in the world. However, in this instance you are forgetting that this constitutional court was an integral part of that very system of governance in which political forces which supported unitarisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina existed. There was a tendency for it to become a sovereign, independent country, and this all came as a result of the Croat-Muslim coalition's activities aimed to this end. These activities fully violated the interests of the Serb nation, because the Serb nation, together with Croats, was a constituent nation. They created together with the Croats their own joint state in 1918, whereas in 1945 they agreed to become peoples in the Bosnia-Herzegovina, which at the time was a federal unit. And living in a federal unit means that they lived in the same area, within the wider sense, with other members of the Serb peoples. The same thing applied to Croats, who agreed to live under the same roof with other Croats living elsewhere in Yugoslavia. The tendency to proclaim Bosnia and Herzegovina a sovereign state would mean the separation of Serbs and Croats from their mother states, namely, Serbia and Croatia, which in turn represents a direct attack on the integrity of Serb and Croat people. The government and government organs are all part of the same system. I would like now to remind you about the chronology of everything that was done to further this tendency to create a unitarian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Please stop there. That wasn't what I was asking you, I was asking you about 1992, not 1918 and not 1945. Do you understand that? Yes or no. Do you understand what I'm asking you?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, but I hope that you also understand that certain things cannot be explained if you don't understand the essence and previous state. Everything has its cause, just as everything has its consequence. One cannot analyse the cause without analysing the consequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That is understood by everybody, Professor, but do stick to the questions that counsel is asking. So just answer his questions. That way we shall get on much faster.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All I'm suggesting to you, Professor, is that in your report you have quoted only from the constitutions themselves and you have completely ignored constitutional court decisions on those constitutions. That's all I'm suggesting to you. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you have, in effect, ignored completely the decision of the highest court in Bosnia, in a sovereign country, which annulled the declaration of the Republika Srpska and is completely opposed to your point of view. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's no interpretation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We are not -- excuse me, Witness. We are not getting any interpretation. Can the question perhaps be repeated so that the witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the interpretation from this headset now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We can all hear the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question, Professor, and I'll ask you to concentrate on the question, answer that question and try to keep it as brief as possible. The question I asked you was and you have in effect completely ignored the highest court -- a decision of the highest court in Bosnia, a sovereign country, which annulled the declaration of the Republika Srpska and a decision which is completely opposed to your point of view. Do you agree with the fact that you ignored it?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. But at the same time, I have to remind you of the following, esteemed Mr. Prosecutor, that you keep forgetting that this constitutional court, as I said when there was no interpretation, that this constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina constitutes an integral part of the authorities that were striving towards creating a unitary state, an independent, sovereign state. After all, you yourself mentioned in your original question that this was a sovereign state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Serb people could not accept that because in this way it would separate itself from the other members of its own people. It is not correct that I only referred to constitutional texts, because in that case my report would have probably been 70 per cent shorter. I mentioned all other relevant documents that you do not refer to here, and I would kindly ask that these other relevant legal documents be dwelt upon as well, because they would also shed more light on the overall situation in the best possible way, and in this way we would get to the truth. And the truth, as Liveus [phoen] said in Roman antiquity, the truth can be concealed, but it cannot be buried altogether. That is the motto of this Honourable Court, I'm sure, and I'm sure the Prosecutors are guided by this lofty motto, but allow me to say that I am guided by it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So the answer to the last question is yes, is it?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, along with the addition I made, and please take into account what I added to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So in effect, your report was misleading by leaving out viewpoints which are opposed to yours, including those of the constitutional court of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't think that it is misleading, because original documents clearly show the different tendencies of the Croats and Muslims as a coalition and the interests of the Serb people, who proclaimed their sovereignty. I think that this presupposes or requires that something be said about the right to self-determination, which you regrettably do not raise. And all of this cannot be understood apart from that. And I think that everybody knows that the right to self-determination is guaranteed in a large number of international legal documents, starting with the UN charter from 1945 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Professor, we are aware that you have a great wealth of knowledge, and we respect that, but this is a criminal trial, and that is why we have lawyers on both sides simply asking questions. And I did explain that your report was filed and it has been received by the Trial Chamber. So please just answer the questions. The Prosecution can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As a constitutional lawyer, you were aware, weren't you, of the Badinter commission?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That was the conference -- an arbitration -- on Yugoslavia, established by the European community, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the international legal aspect of this subject-matter, and I'm not an expert in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It was a commission established by the European community, headed by a French lawyer, Mr. Badinter, and comprising Judges of the constitutional courts of Germany, Belgium, Italy, and Spain. Do you agree with that -- are you aware of that, I mean?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: To a considerable degree, from news reports and television reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You're aware of it from newspaper reports. Are you saying you haven't seen the opinions published by the Badinter commission on the break-up of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I said that this belongs to international law. That aspect. And it is not directly related to this particular subject-matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It hasn't stopped you expressing some opinions on international law in your report, has it, Professor?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What are you precisely referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: One point you say that you were -- at one point you make an opinion as to whether or not Bosnia-Herzegovina is a sovereign state, don't you? It's at paragraph 56 of your report. I read from it: "As a complex state formation Bosnia-Herzegovina is a state of international relations while -- are not. However, it is not a sovereign state, as the international community has limited in certain elements." You agree there that you are expressing an opinion on international law, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would not agree that this is an opinion on international law. I think that it is the simplest possible fact that could be ascertained. It has to do with the Dayton constitution and with the adoption of the Dayton constitution, and a series of related problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I asked you earlier whether you had seen the Badinter reports. Is your answer that you haven't seen the Badinter reports?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly, because I read quite a few of these things as a citizen and as a scholar. But I don't know what your question is specifically, so if you would be so kind as to put a specific question to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Specifically, in the second Badinter opinion, on the 11th of January, 1992, Lord Carrington submitted the following question to the commission: "Does the Serbian population in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, as one of the constituent peoples of Yugoslavia, have the right to self-determination." Badinter commission --

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- reported that the -- that was a question submitted. Are you aware of the question submitted by Lord Carrington of the Badinter commission which is directly on the topic that you're giving evidence about?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you aware - I'm asking you - of the question submitted by Lord Carrington to the Badinter commission, which is a question directly on the topic you're giving evidence about? Are you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I assume that this will be followed by your substantive question, so please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether you are aware that Lord Carrington submitted that question to the Badinter commission. That's the question you're giving evidence about in your report.

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, please, could we look at the core of the matter? Can we look at the substantive question behind this? It is so irrelevant whether I know that or not. What is important is that you put your real question to me so that I could give you an answer related to the right to self-determination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As a constitutional expert, you've come to this Trial Chamber to give evidence on the constitutional issues involving the break-up of the former Yugoslavia and the constitutional validity or otherwise of the Republika Srpska and the Federation; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it was not my understanding that it is the break-up of Yugoslavia that is highly relevant in these proceedings, although in my opinion it would be a good thing if this were to be discussed. But the question is the establishment of Republika Srpska and relations within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You have expressed an opinion, and a fairly strong opinion, I'd suggest, on whether the Serbs, as a constituent nation of Yugoslavia, had a right to self-determination. What I'm asking you is: Are you aware that the very same question was considered by the Badinter commission in January 1992, which is the time frame if which you're giving evidence about here today?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As for my opinion, it is not important whether Badinter's commission discussed this or not. I can have my own views that may fully coincide with those of that commission, or they can be quite divergent.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how many times I have to ask the same question. I'm asking you only whether you are aware of the question that was considered by the Badinter commission. Can you please give me an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This is probably the fourth time that I'm saying that I do not see the point of this question. I would appreciate it if you would put a direct question to me as to what I think about the right to self-determination and whether I know what one person or another person thought about this can be of great importance, lesser importance, or no importance whatsoever, as far as my personal views are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It's clear that the witness won't give a direct answer, so can you move on, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As the Trial Chamber pleases.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I take it from your last answer you don't know, so I'll give you the answer. The Badinter commission found -- this is the French, Belgian, German, Italian, and Spanish constitutional Judges deliberating on the question of self-determination in Yugoslavia, and specifically in Bosnia, held: "It is well established, whatever the circumstances, the right to self-determination must not involve changes to --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down. The reading is too fast for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can you please read it slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will read it slowly, Your Honour, "The right to self-determination must not involve changes to existing frontiers at the time of independence (uti pucidatus juris) [phoen], except where the states concerned agree otherwise." That was the conclusion they came to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know why you insist on that, whether I know or do not know. You should be interested in my opinion. As for the scope of my knowledge regarding other people's opinions, that's a different matter altogether. Excuse me, but it is becoming increasingly embarrassing for me to have to say this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't wish to embarrass you, Professor. All I'm asking you about is the fact that the Badinter commission looked into the very issues that you are here giving evidence about today, looked into these issues, made conclusions, published them, they were accepted by the European community, and you haven't mentioned them.

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't think that I have to mention everything in my report, because this would then be a great big book. I was asked to present my own opinion on a particular case, the right to self-determination. I spoke about that, and I wish I could say a few words about it today. There were divergent views, though. The Badinter commission then in various circles among the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Yugoslavia, Croatia, et cetera, and generally speaking, the right to self-determination over the past several years was the subject of major discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In your report at paragraph 20, you said finally the right to self-declaration as absolutely incontestable is pledged by international documents as well. You haven't actually mentioned what those international documents are, Professor, so we haven't been able to check what they are. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what international documents absolutely incontestably allow the right to declaration?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I did not mention them because I believe that this was general knowledge and that anybody dealing with constitutional law, let alone international law, is aware of that. This is first and foremost the UN charter of 1945. And then also another very important document is the covenant on economic, social, and political rights from 1976.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Professor. If I could ask you one little question on this. For sure, self-determination is mentioned in both the UN charter and the international covenant on civil and political rights of 1976, but it is somewhat controversial. It isn't that straightforward, I don't think. Is it a right of states or of peoples within a state? I just have a simple question, though, for you, which is if there is a rule of customary international law based on state practice and opinio juris that peoples in colonial or neocolonial situations. Peoples before independence have a right, if we are dealing with a state of an independent state, whether it's a unitary state or a federal state or a confederation, what are the criteria for the people to put forward that they have a legitimate right at international law to self-determination and therefore to secede? And if you could give me or give the Trial Chamber your view on that very succinctly, I think that would be very much appreciated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I appreciate the fact that you have put this question. First and foremost, it is not the right of states to self-determination, because one could hardly speak of that; isn't that right? Because if the independence of a state is jeopardised, then it is not a question of the self-determination of that state, but it is the defence of its national and state independence. We are talking about the right of peoples to self-determination. Some people say of nations. Self-determination of nations or peoples, the right to self-determination, including the right to secession, is referred to in the mentioned international documents, and it is considered to be a major democratic achievement of contemporary civilisation. By your leave, and I assume that this is what you asked for yourself, I would like to present my opinion. A major achievement of the democratic civilisation is the proclamation of the sovereignty of peoples and nations. The sovereignty of peoples, as is a well-known fact, and university students can give an answer to that. That is a general thing. That is the right of a people, of a certain state, of the citizens of a certain state, to elect the government under which they are going to live. But national sovereignty does not correspond with that type of sovereignty. National sovereignty means the right to self-determination, precisely. That is to say that the nation maintains its national integrity and identity within a state entity, within the state entity within which it wishes to live, either within the existing state or within another independent state, and so on. May I add, in passing, that the right of a people or a nation to self-determination exclusively pertains to a nation people, not to national minorities. Therefore, if the Serb people - and I assume that we have all agreed on that - that was my understanding, just like the Croat people, and after the 1970s, after the communist regime, Tito's regime, Josip Broz Tito gave them this right, this characteristic. That is to say the Muslim people became a people too, then all these three peoples have the right to self-determination, including the right to secession. That is where the core of the problem lies. However, unfortunately we did not manage to understand each other properly, the gentleman, the Prosecutor and I, that is to say, why the Serb people wanted to avoid the creation of a unitary state and the proclamation of a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina. They wanted to remain within Bosnia-Herzegovina and Bosnia-Herzegovina within the joint state of Yugoslavia, in which in other areas the Serb people live, the Croat people live, not to mention all the peoples of the former Yugoslavia. So that is the core of the problem as regards the right to self-determination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you for your response, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your thesis -- excuse me for a moment. Your thesis is that the referendum held by the Serbs was constitutionally legitimate, but the referendum held by the Bosnian government wasn't; is that correct, constitutionally correct?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I did not speak specifically about the referendum that was held in Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole, but I referred to the referendum that had to do with the creation of the new Serb state, Republika Srpska. This referendum stems from this very right of people for self-determination. If Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as a constituent nation --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I was just asking you --

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You interrupt me quite frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I was asking you a simple question whether your thesis, that is, the bones of what you were saying, is that what the Bosnian government did was unconstitutional but what the Serbian people did was constitutional. It's not a difficult question, surely.

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. A very simplified question, and I agree with what you said, which is that the Serb people, through their legitimate and legally elected representatives, enacted certain documents and took certain steps that brought about the creation of Republika Srpska. I believe this to be legal and legitimate, whereas the other one I don't believe to be legal and legitimate because it violated the consensus which lies in the core of the relationships that existed in Bosnia and Herzegovina, where three constituent peoples live. If we have three constituent peoples, then there must be a consensus among them in order to ensure equality. The violation of consensus, regardless of to whose detriment it was done, whether to the detriment of Muslims, Croats, or Serbs, is something that cannot be considered legal or legitimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you aware that following the Serb referendum, the Bosnian government -- or sorry, the Badinter commission considered the issue of whether or not the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina should be recognised internationally? Are you aware of that? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This is the same question like the one you put to me before. I would like to ask you to describe what I think about the essence of this subject-matter. Now, whether I know something or not will become obvious based on the answer that I will give you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it's a simple question whether he's aware or not of the Badinter commission. That's not responsive to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Professor. I think you must understand what the question is and then you simply answer. He's not asking you to agree with the contents of that report of the Badinter commission. He's simply asking you whether you are aware of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to give my opinion. I don't want to be asked whether I know about something. And then once I give you my explanation, then it will become obvious whether I am aware of something or not. I don't see why this is being insisted upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That is how the questions should be answered, Professor, and the Trial Chamber orders you to answer. If you're not aware of anything that is put to you by the Prosecution, you say you're not aware. If you are, you say so. It does not mean that you agree with whatever the contents of that particular decision are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So you're not aware that the referendum sponsored by the government on February 29, March 1, 1992, was held at the suggestion of the Badinter commission? And I quote from the opinion number 4, 11th of January, 1992, paragraph 4: "In these circumstances, the arbitration commission is of the opinion that the will of the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina to constitute the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a sovereign and independent state cannot be held to have been fully established. This assessment could be reviewed if appropriate guarantees were provided by the republic applying for recognition, possibly by means of a referendum, of all the citizens of the SRBH without distinction, carried out under international supervision."

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct, that the referendum was organised under international supervision, with participation of representatives of all three constituent peoples. Yes, that's all fine. However, if one nation does not participate in it, then this referendum cannot be either legal or legitimate. Because, as I've just told you, this violates the consensus that can be found in the essence of their inter-relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I want to suggest to you is that the two referendums were very, very different, weren't they? I'll explain why to you they were very different. The referendum for the Serb people had two different ballot papers, didn't it, one for Serbs and one for non-Serbs? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But the referendum which was internationally supervised and sponsored by the Bosnia government in relation to independence was a referendum with only one ballot paper for everyone, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The -- and as a constitutional expert, you, of course, would recognise and respect the judgements of this Tribunal, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In the Tadic judgement of the 7th of May, 1997, I just want to read to you what the Trial Chamber found after hearing evidence about the Serb ballot in November 1991. I'm reading from paragraph 99: "In November 1991 --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please read slowly because the interpreters do not have the original text.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: "In November 1991 the SDS sponsored, organised, and conducted a plebiscite primarily for the benefit of the Bosnian Serb population. Voters were given different ballots depending on whether they were Serb or non-Serb. The difference between the two ballots was significant. For Bosnian Serbs the ballot asked: Are you in favour of the decision reached by the assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 24th of October, 1991, whereby the Serbian people should remain in the common state of Yugoslavia, which would include Serbia, Montenegro, Serb autonomous region Krajina, Serb autonomous region Slovinka-Krajina [phoen], Western Srem, along with others willing to remain in such a state. While the question for non-Serbs was: Are you in favour of Bosnia and Herzegovina remaining a republic with equal status in a common state of Yugoslavia, with all the other republics, which also declare themselves willing to do so?" Prosecution Exhibit 97. The great majority who did vote were Serbs. Those Serbs who did not being branded as traitors. Most non-Serbs regarded the plebiscite as directed only to Serbs. The Trial Chamber goes on, "The outcome of the plebiscite purported to be a hundred per cent in favour. The SDS leadership --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The SDS leadership used this outcome as a basis on which to develop the separate Serb political structure. The plebiscite was cited as justification for all subsequent moves such as the ultimate walkout of the SDS representatives from the Bosnia and Herzegovina assembly. The various negotiations conducted at the federal and international levels and the proclamation on the 9th of January 1992 of the republic of the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was, "Used as a pretext, as an excuse, explanation, for everything they did. "Also, on the basis of the plebiscite, the SDS and military forces in each region, including the JNA, paramilitary organisations, local TO units, and special police units began to establish physical and political control over certain municipalities where it had not already gained control by virtue of the elections. In these regions, which included opstina Prijedor, the SDS representatives in public office in some cases established parallel municipal governments and separate police forces. Physical control was asserted by positioning military units, tanks, and heavy artillery around the municipalities and setting up checkpoints to control the movement of non-Serbs." That's what the Trial Chamber found in the case of Tadic in relation to that ballot. Is there anything -- were you aware of that, and is there anything you could disagree with there?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I did not have an opportunity to read the Tadic judgement. I don't even know whether that was published in Belgrade. However, as regards the plebiscite that was held on the 9th and 10th of November, 1991, I can say that this was simply a confirmation. I think that I read somewhere that 96.something per cent expressed the support for the enactments and measures that had been taken by -- until that time by the Serb assembly in order to create Republika Srpska, which later on was done on the 9th of January, 1992 by proclaiming the declaration. I believe this referendum to be fully legal and legitimate, because, like in all other democratic countries, when people express their will at a referendum, that is a legal expected measure, and we saw that this was done in this case as well. You said that -- it is true what you said, that there were different formulations on the ballots but this was an opportunity for representatives of other peoples to express their opinion regarding the coexistence in that area, because the first ballot applied only to the members of the Serb people. However, this was an opportunity for others who lived there to express their opinion regarding their future life together, and I believe that to have been appropriate as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The conduct of the -- or the circumstances surrounding the second referendum were very different, and I quote to you from "Bosnia, a short history," by Noel Malcolm, the updated edition 1996, at page 230, where he says that "The army was not impartial or unpolitical, was made evident on 29th February and 1st of March when the referendum was held in Bosnia. While Karadzic's SDS forbade Serbs to vote in the referendum and erected road blocks to prevent ballot boxes entering the areas of Bosnia it controlled, federal army planes dropped leaflets supporting --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: "-- dropped leaflets supporting the boycott. Roughly 64 per cent of the electorate did vote. However, including many thousands of Serbs in the major cities on a ballot paper which asked: Are you in favour of a sovereign and independent Bosnia-Herzegovina, a state of equal citizens and nations of Muslims, Serbs, Croats, and others who live in it? Almost unanimously, they voted yes." My question is: Were you aware of the circumstances surrounding the conduct of that ballot in February/March 1992, as described by Mr. Malcolm?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I have not read that book. But what you just read out pertains to the factual situation. What was ordered by Mr. Karadzic or somebody else, or what was done by them is something that I did not cover in my report. It is not a constitutional, legal question; it is a factual question that naturally needs to be discussed in a certain way. But I don't see that how I could have contributed to that within my report. I did not live in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time, and I am not aware of factual situation of what -- who did what, regardless of which side they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Yugoslavian constitution in force in early 1992, and of course the Republika Srpska constitutions and the Socialist Republic constitutions, none of those authorised one nationality or ethnicity to establish parallel governments, did they?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: These are very different constitutions. Yugoslav constitution from 1992 was adopted during the dictatorship of Milosevic, whereas socialist constitutions of other republics, including Serbia, all of these constitutions were passed in 1974. Yugoslavia had a constitution of this nature in 1974. Now, I'm not quite sure what you want me to do. Do you want me to compare these constitutions, or what exactly would you like me to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the constitutional expert, Professor. I just asked you simply, or put to you the proposition that none of those constitutions authorised a nation to set up a separate government or a parallel government, did they?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This is not contained in any constitution in this world.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And of course, none of those constitutions authorised the Bosnian Serbs to forcibly take control of any towns, cities, or villages throughout Bosnia, did they?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. These constitutions do not envision that. But the constitution from 1974 saw Bosnia and Herzegovina only as a federal unit and status of a federal unit within a federal state is well known. You can see examples of that in Canada, in Switzerland, and so on. So none of these states can proclaim their independence or secede or do something else. People can proclaim that, but after that, the issue of borders needs to be established. If you are setting up discussion along these lines, and if you are denying the right to Serb people to self-determination, then we will find ourselves in front of a very delicate question, which is that this can bring us to a conclusion, and a wrong one at that, namely, the conclusion that Slovenes, Croats, Macedonians, did not have a right to self-determination. They did not have a right to secede and establish their own states. And then this would be followed by the next conclusion, which is that the current Slovenia, current Croatia, current Macedonia are illegal states in fact. However, Slovenes as a separate nation, Croats as a separate nation, and Macedonians too, did had a right to self-determination and they did create their own independent sovereign states. What could have presented a problem -- well please allow me to complete my answer. Please to not interrupt me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no. Witness, you have gone outside the question that counsel asked you, so that's why you are being stopped.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was such that I had to present my answer. Could you please put a more specific question to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't think I can be any more specific than asking you which of the constitutions authorised Serbs to forcibly take control of towns, cities, or villages. That's fairly specific, I think. I'm just suggesting to you that none of them authorised the Serbs to forcibly take control, that is, with arms, villages, towns, cities, or municipalities, did they?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Then I can ask you this: Which constitution was it that authorised Slovenes, Croats, and Macedonians to start creating their own states? It's the same matter. You are ignoring this fact, and you should not do that. You should have that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Witness, you're not here to ask counsel questions. You are here to answer the questions. And just stick to the questions asked by counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The -- excuse me for a moment. You would agree that the constitution of the Serb republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina contained a fairly impressive set of human rights guarantees, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The first one which was proclaimed on the 16th of March, 1992 contains some fairly impressive articles on human rights and freedoms under article 2 you have a copy there in front of you I take it. "Article 12, freedom and personal safety of men are inviolable. No one can be deprived of or limited in his freedom except in cases in compliance with the procedures provided for by law."

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a classical formulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: "14, no one may be subject to torture, cruel, inhumane or humiliating treatment or punishment. Any extortion of confession or statements shall be forbidden and punishable."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please read slower. It is impossible to follow this pace.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, counsel. Slow down so that they can interpret what you are reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The second part, I'll reread it. "Article 14, no one may be subjected to torture, cruel, inhuman or humiliating treatment or punishment. Any extortion of confession or statements shall be forbidden and punishable. It is forbidden to conduct --" I won't go into that one. "Article 15, unlawful deprivation of freedom is punishable. No one may be deprived of freedom without a court decision, which must be stated and handed to the person at the time of deprivation of freedom. A person suspected of having committed a criminal offence can be detained only if it is indispensable for the conduct of criminal proceedings or for the safety of people. A detention has to be as short as possible. Pursuant to the decision of a first instance court the detention may last two months at the most. Republic supreme court may extend it for another 2 months." It guarantees the right to free trial in article 18. Freedom of movement, article 21. Freedom of religion, article 28. Article 30, the right to peaceful assembly and peaceful protest. Article 31, freedom of political association and activity in compliance with the law shall be guaranteed. Article 39, forced labour shall be prohibited. Article 47, human rights and freedoms shall be restricted only by equal rights and freedoms enjoyed by others and by the need to protect universal human values and democratic accomplishments. Article 48, the rights and freedoms guaranteed by this constitution cannot be denied or restricted. Abuse or freedom and rights is unconstitutional and punishable. You know this document very well, don't you professor?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I believe I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Nothing in this authorises the forcible takeover by the military or paramilitaries of a municipality, does it?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And if people were to do so, it would be unconstitutional, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Nothing allows -- nothing authorises the establishment of extra judicial detention centres for the detention of non-Serbs, does it?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Certainly, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And to do so, to establish extra judicial detention centres for non-Serbs would be unconstitutional, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Mr. Re, but for the sake of clarification, on page 113, your question on line 20, "nothing in this authorises the forcible takeover by the military or paramilitaries of a municipality, does it?" The witness's answer is "yes." I think it should be clarified. Does he mean yes, I'm agreeing with you, or contra?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. I agree. I agree. The constitution does not authorise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And in order telling non-Serbs that they had to wear white armbands would be contrary to this constitution too, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And so would an order preventing more than three Muslims from meeting, that would be unconstitutional too, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And punishable under this constitution?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So would an order forbidding political parties. That would also be unconstitutional?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As would the proclamation of a state of emergency preventing citizens from leaving a municipality. That too would be unconstitutional, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Which provision is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's not there, and I'm suggesting that an order proclaiming a state of emergency which prevents citizens from leaving a municipality under that constitution with its model human rights provisions would be unconstitutional, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That requires a broader discussion, because imminent threat of war or a state of war always calls for extraordinary measures. So this is a factual question. It has to do with regulations in the country concerned. As for all the rest that you mentioned, I fully agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And of course, isolating an order, isolating all people of Croatian nationality to be isolated and taken to vital facilities, that is, Croats, would also be contrary to this constitution, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the way it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And of course forced labour, which I mentioned earlier, would be contrary to the constitution?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And more so if it was at the frontline, doing things like digging trenches. It would be ultra-unconstitutional, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So would the looting of non-Serb properties by Muslims and Croats forced into labour. That would also be unconstitutional, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Any looting is unlawful and illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A Municipal Assembly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution, you've consumed your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Of one hour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I have. Not in questions, Your Honour. I think in answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no. It's the whole time put together.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I appreciate under Rule 98, the Prosecution is supposed to put its case to an expert witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's not the contention. It's just the time that we have come to the end of today's proceedings. Mr. Pantelic, you had indicated that the witness was required to leave, but we can start in the morning with him and complete his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that it's very, very complicated question. I think we have to finish with this witness today. I have only a couple of questions, not more than five or ten minutes, so we could -- I do apologise to our colleagues from interpreters' booth. They are working very hard today. But if maybe one break of ten minutes or fifteen minutes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to suggest that. I was wondering whether that would be accepted by the interpreters. Have a ten-minute break so that we can complete this witness today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm asking the interpreters. Can we have an answer?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters kindly ask that we finish within the next ten minutes and we go on working that way, rather than reschedule the entire afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think we can proceed. Mr. -- the Prosecution can wind up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The takeover of a municipality by one ethnicity, forcing out the others, would be contrary to the constitution of the Republika Srpska, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel speak in the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't pick your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The takeover of municipality by one ethnicity forcing out the others, one nation, would be contrary to the constitution of the Republika Srpska, wouldn't it? You're nodding. Are you saying yes?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Correct. Any democratic constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... takeover of a municipality by one ethnicity, such as the Serbs, and taking over the government and preventing the others from participating in the government would also be unconstitutional, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You are right. Any discrimination on national grounds is anti-constitutional, anti-civilisation, and inhumane, and contrary to international legal documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As would, of course, an article in a municipality -- sorry - a decision to establish a municipality assembly which allowed only Serbian Democratic Party deputies and other deputies of Serb ethnicity to participate, that would also be unconstitutional, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Any discrimination on national grounds is absolutely unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm referring here specifically to Article 5 of Exhibit P124, the Official Gazette of the municipality --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm referring specifically here to Article 5 of P124, the Official Gazette of the municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel, please. Yes. You're finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And one suggestion, Your Honour. If my friend wish to make some certain reference to Article 5, I think it would be fair enough to show to professor this particular Official Gazette, this act, and this Article 5, and then he can make his opinion. Otherwise there is no sense in the transcript. My learned friend Mr. Re said, "I'm referring here specifically to Article 5," but professor didn't see Article 5. So he was not able to even give a comment, as well as the Defence, of course. So maybe we can put on the ELMO and one copy in B/C/S language in front of professor and then we shall hear the proper answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, in order to put the Prosecution case to the professor, I was intending to take him through about 20 exhibits in this trial, the various orders of the municipality of Bosanski Samac, or the Crisis Staff of the War Presidency, but the one hour didn't permit me the time to do so, and the length -- the answers didn't allow me to do so either. So in that respect, I haven't taken him through each of the documents which I wished to and asked him to comment on them. He said they're all unconstitutional -- the extracts I've read from, or the effect of them. So in my submission, if it's good for one, it's good for all of them and I should be permitted to go back and show all of them to him again. There are other documents I intend to tender. I won't necessarily do it at the moment because again for time considerations, I intend to tender the constitution and the Badinter commission reports. And again for time reasons, not having the time in the hour to get the witness to look at them and to comment, I haven't shown them to him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber is of the view that the time taken and explanations of the witness are sufficient. I don't think there is any more reason why we should spend more time with this witness. So we'll go ahead with the re-examination. The Prosecution can always produce the documents they wanted to produce.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you mean to tender the documents into evidence, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. If I can do that, maybe after Mr. Pantelic finishes, to allow the witness to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Because that can be done at any stage. It doesn't have to be today. Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Well, it's, I mean, quite -- situation. Now I would like to see this Exhibit P124 and finally this Article 5, so that we know about we are talking here. Otherwise it is not fair for Defence expert witness just to put him a question what is in Article 5 of I don't know which decision. Even I'm not so familiar. And then we shall see whether something is in accordance or against the constitutional law principles. That was the proper way, and that was the idea of my intervention. And I would kindly ask my learned friend to make a specific reference, because this is Official Gazette, of course, what -- which article we have to find, because there is a lot of decisions and orders here. Contains each of them Article 5. So on which Article 5 and which decision you particular is referring, so in order to clarify this thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, that's not difficult. It's quite simply P124, it's page 5. It's the -- headed, as I said for the benefit of the Trial Chamber "Decision to establish an assembly of the Serbian people of the municipality of Bosanski Samac." And it's Article 5 of that, which is at the top of page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You mean Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo information? Is that? So because there are many things like that. Okay. So Article 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, could you please read out the -- read out Article 5 of this decision on establishing the assembly of the Serbian people, and could you tell us whether there is anything unconstitutional about it.

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could now the representative of the Prosecution put his question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sir, but I am asking you now. So can you tell me whether the formulation of Article 5 has any unconstitutional -- anything unconstitutional about it?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It depends on the ethnic composition of the municipality. If the assembly man of the SDS were elected democratically, then I don't see anything unconstitutional about it. However, this is a factual question, and I now cannot decide, cannot assess whether they were elected democratically or in any other way. This is beyond my expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You can take these exhibits. I don't need your assistance. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My next question, Professor, is as follows: My colleague mentioned these famous decisions passed by constitutional courts. My first question is this: In view of the fact that the Serb people left all political institutions and organs of government in 1992, can you tell us what was the composition of the courts in Bosnia and Herzegovina, for example, in November of 1992, when this constitutional court passed its decision? What was the ethnic composition of these organs, and did this constitutional court in fact represent a body that, following the principles accepted in Bosnia, had within it representatives of all three constituent peoples?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I now cannot tell you what was the composition of the assembly, the government, the constitutional court, and other organs, but what I know is that that was the period of time when members of the Serb nation did not participate in the work of these organs. Therefore, the decisions passed by these organs cannot be considered legally valid because, as I've mentioned several times, this violated the core, or the substantive element or principle that required that there be a consensus, an equality among the three constituent peoples. If any nation, be it Serb nation, Croat nation, or Muslim nation, does not participate in the work of any organ, be it assembly or constitutional court, and so on, then the work of that body is not legally valid, let alone constitutional.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My next question -- and this is something that you mentioned in your report. You mentioned the constitutional court based on the Dayton constitution. This is the constitutional court of Bosnia and Herzegovina , which also has foreign justices. I'm asking you this now: Why is it that in the constitutional court of Bosnia and Herzegovina there are justices who are foreign nationals? What is your explanation for this?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This question should be put to authors of the Dayton constitution. It is obvious that this was an expression of mistrust that main protagonists, meaning the international community, had when the constitution was drafted, and they obviously mistrusted the ability of people in Bosnia and Herzegovina to respect consensus. This is why they wanted to ensure the presence and active participation of prominent judges, among whom was one of my good friends, Professor Louis Favere, from France. They basically wanted to ensure that there wouldn't be any bias present.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that, unlike other former Yugoslav republics, Bosnia and Herzegovina had three constituent peoples living in it then, tell us, please, this: If one of the constituent peoples leaves all government organs, then does the old Bosnia and Herzegovina, in its old form, continue to exist?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, because this is a precondition for continual existence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. At the time, Bosnia and Herzegovina was -- or had a status of a federal unit, and this same would apply to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. In 1992, its constitution was adopted by the rump assembly of SFRY, without participation of MPs from Slovenia, Croatia, Macedonia, and so on, and I believe that that constitution was legally not valid, and this is something that I stated in my opinion. The same would apply to the situation you described in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now let me ask you this. A referendum was scheduled for late February/early March of 1992 by that rump Bosnia and Herzegovina, and now, can you tell us whether this referendum was legally valid?

utterances.speaker: PAVLE NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If this was a referendum in which only members of Croat and Muslim nations participated, and not those of Serb nation, then that referendum cannot be legally valid or legitimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I've finished with my examination, Your Honour. Thank you. [Interpretation] Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor, for giving evidence to this Tribunal. You are now free. You can go. The Trial Chamber wishes to thank the supporting services, the interpreters, the recording systems, the court reporters, for their patience. We are now finished for this afternoon. We'll adjourn until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 13th day of November, 2002, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.30 p.m.,
